title: Consistency.UnusedSuppression flags directives that ARE actively suppressing findings
description:
Mirrors GitHub issue #29: https://github.com/TAJD/cofferdam/issues/29

SUMMARY
Consistency.UnusedSuppression reports cofferdam-ignore-file: <CheckId> directives as 'stale' (covering no findings) when in fact the directives are doing real work — removing them surfaces the very findings the directive said it wasn't suppressing.

Correctness issue with real downstream consequences: actively misleads users (and LLM agents) into removing load-bearing suppressions. Reporter caught it only by re-running cofferdam after the cleanup and noticing 76 newly-reported findings.

REPRO (the actual sequence hit)
In a Next.js + shadcn/ui project, components/ui/index.ts (the shadcn barrel) had at the top:
  // cofferdam-ignore-file: Warning.UnusedImport: shadcn barrel — primitives are intentionally re-exported regardless of current consumers
  // cofferdam-ignore-file: Design.OrphanExport: same — barrel is the public API surface
  // ... ~80 re-exports across 17 shadcn primitive files

cofferdam 0.3.0 reported on lines 1-2:
  [Consistency.UnusedSuppression] suppression directive for Warning.UnusedImport covers no findings — the directive is stale
  [Consistency.UnusedSuppression] suppression directive for Design.OrphanExport covers no findings — the directive is stale

Removed both lines. Re-ran. Result: 76 NEW findings — all Warning.UnusedImport on ./components/ui/index.ts (Badge, Button, ... 76 total).

The directive HAD been suppressing exactly those 76 findings. The 'covers no findings' claim was factually wrong. Restoring the suppressions made the 76 vanish again. Reproducible.

HYPOTHESIS
Suppression directives hide findings from being reported at scan time entirely. baseline.json contains zero entries for those 76 sites. The suppression is the only thing suppressing them.

UnusedSuppression then asks the post-suppression view 'are there findings here that I'm covering?' — gets 'no' because the suppression already removed them. Tautology: a successful suppression always looks unused if you check after it has filtered. The check is asking the wrong question — it needs to compare *pre-suppression* findings against the directive scope, not post-suppression.

FIX
1. Track a 'would have fired here' set during scanning. Suppression directives consume from that set. UnusedSuppression checks the consumed-count, not the post-filter findings.
2. If (1) is too expensive: drop UnusedSuppression entirely until the underlying signal is reliable. False positives that drive users to delete real suppressions are worse than no check at all.

IMPACT
Reporter wasted ~15 minutes plus a downstream cofferdam run figuring out what happened, then had to restore the suppressions and document the bug. An LLM agent following the check's recommendation without re-verifying would have removed the directives, committed, and silently regressed the suppression posture of the repo. The findings only became visible because cofferdam:full was run again, otherwise the regression would have shipped.

ENVIRONMENT
- @cofferdam/cofferdam@0.3.0, @cofferdam/check-sdk@0.3.0
- Node 22.20.0, Windows 11
- Repo layout: shadcn/ui barrel (components/ui/index.ts)

RELATED
Probably interacts with #27 (orphan-export reachability through barrel re-exports) — same shadcn-barrel pattern, different bug surface.
close_reason: Implemented Option D: added CheckMeta.observes_findings flag, split engine finalize into two phases (non-observers, then snapshot, then observers). Only Consistency.UnusedSuppression sets the flag; meta-test enforces. 5 regression tests cover the original symptom + OrphanExport parity + genuine-stale case. Verified: build, test (395 pass, +5), clippy, fmt. Commit on main.

title: [CRITICAL] cofferdam fix Warning.TripleEquals corrupts == null semantics (gh #22)
description:
GitHub: https://github.com/TAJD/cofferdam/issues/22

DATA-LOSS CLASS BUG. `cofferdam fix` rewrites `== null` to `=== null` (and `!= null` to `!== null`). This is the canonical TS idiom that matches BOTH `null` AND `undefined`; the rewritten form matches only `null` and lets `undefined` slip through.

User reports real codebase damage: API route handlers, URL encoders broken silently because tests don't cover the undefined-vs-null discriminator. Shipping these 'fixes' would have introduced 'wm=undefined' params and validators that pass undefined through.

Fix (option 1, cheapest, defensible): exempt `== null` / `!= null` from the TripleEquals autofix. The diagnostic still fires; humans decide null-only vs null-or-undefined.

Option 2: rewrite to `x === null || x === undefined` (verbose but semantically equivalent).

Option 3: defer the entire TripleEquals autofix until type-aware (knows whether undefined is in the value's domain).

Pick option 1 — ESLint's `eqeqeq` rule has shipped `{ null: 'ignore' }` for over a decade for exactly this reason.
close_reason: TripleEquals.autofix now returns None when either operand is the bare null token (recursively strips outer parens, word-boundary safe). Diagnostic still fires; humans decide. 5 unit tests + extended fixture; updated tests/fix.rs to expect 5 edits instead of 3 since the fixture grew.

title: Inline 'cofferdam-ignore <CheckId> — reason' parses as broad suppression and finding still fires (gh #42)
description:
## Summary

Linked to https://github.com/TAJD/cofferdam/issues/42.

The inline directive `// cofferdam-ignore Design.OrphanExport — <reason>` exhibits **two failures simultaneously**:

1. The parser does not bind the check id — `Consistency.BroadSuppression` fires saying "no check id" even though `Design.OrphanExport` is present in the comment.
2. Whether or not the parse binds the id, the underlying `Design.OrphanExport` finding still fires — the suppression does nothing for the line it was meant to silence.

## Version & platform

- cofferdam 0.3.2 (npm `@cofferdam/cofferdam@^0.3.2`)
- x86_64-pc-windows-msvc

## Reproducer (from the gh issue)

```ts
// apps/web/src/App.tsx
import { Routes, Route, Link } from 'react-router-dom'

// cofferdam-ignore Design.OrphanExport — Vite entry (referenced from index.html via main.tsx)
export default function App() {
  // ...
}
```

`cofferdam check` output:

```
── Consistency ───────────────
  [  0] [    info] ./apps/web/src/App.tsx:7:4  Broad `// cofferdam-ignore` (no check id) — narrow it to a specific id and add a reason.  (Consistency.BroadSuppression)

── Design ───────────────
  [  5] [  medium] ./apps/web/src/App.tsx:8:1  default export is exported but never imported in the project  (Design.OrphanExport)
```

## Hypotheses

1. The suppression parser's check-id pattern may require a separator other than space — `:` or `[...]`. The accepted form needs documenting either way.
2. The em-dash (`—`) reason separator may break the parse where a regular dash (`-`) does not — UTF-8 / regex character class issue in the suppression parser.
3. The directive sits on the line above the export and is supposed to bind to "next non-comment line"; if cd-wqc's two-phase finalize change reordered something, the bound-line may be off-by-one.

## Acceptance

- [ ] `// cofferdam-ignore Design.OrphanExport — reason` (em-dash) parses, binds the id, and suppresses the finding on the next non-comment line.
- [ ] `// cofferdam-ignore Design.OrphanExport - reason` (ASCII hyphen) does the same.
- [ ] `// cofferdam-ignore Design.OrphanExport: reason` does the same.
- [ ] When the directive successfully binds a check id, `Consistency.BroadSuppression` does NOT fire on that directive.
- [ ] `Consistency.UnusedSuppression` correctly distinguishes "directive that successfully suppressed" from "directive that parsed but matched nothing" — no spurious unused-suppression noise on the fix.
- [ ] The error message on `Consistency.BroadSuppression` shows the canonical syntax inline (cd-cmb-style hint), so users don't have to grep docs to find the accepted form.
- [ ] Suppression integration tests added covering: (a) each separator variant, (b) directive immediately above and on the same line as the target, (c) `cofferdam-ignore-next-line` parity if that form is also supported.

## Related

- gh #42
- cd-1c7 (plugin findings through suppression pipeline)
- cd-wqc (two-phase finalize for suppression observability)
- `crates/cofferdam-engine/src/suppress.rs`
- Reporter repo (private): `C:\Users\tajdi\poker-puzzle` (Vite + React + Cloudflare Workers)
close_reason: Space-separator next-line form now binds the check id via the looks_like_check_id heuristic (Category.Name-shaped first token after the marker); reason separators \(em-dash, ASCII hyphen, colon\) all work because only the first whitespace token is consumed. BroadSuppression and UnusedSuppression both consult the same heuristic so the directive flows consistently through the engine. 14 new unit tests + verified end-to-end against the gh #42 repro.

title: public_api.exports doesn't suppress Design.OrphanExport on exact-file entries (gh #41)
description:
## Summary

Linked to https://github.com/TAJD/cofferdam/issues/41.

A file whose path appears **as an exact string** in `[public_api].exports` in `cofferdam.invariants.toml` still produces `Design.OrphanExport` findings. Glob entries (`apps/web/src/routes/**`) appear to suppress correctly. This is the documented purpose of the section — exact entries must work too.

## Version & platform

- cofferdam 0.3.2 (npm `@cofferdam/cofferdam@^0.3.2`)
- x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, Node 22.20.0, pnpm 10.18.3

## Reproducer (from the gh issue)

```toml
[public_api]
exports = [
  "apps/web/src/main.tsx",
  "apps/web/src/App.tsx",
  "apps/web/src/routes/**",
  "apps/worker/src/index.ts",
  "apps/worker/src/routes/**",
  "apps/worker/src/middleware/**",
  "apps/worker/src/glicko.ts",
]
```

Findings still fire on `apps/web/src/App.tsx`, `apps/worker/src/index.ts`, and `apps/worker/src/glicko.ts` despite each being an exact-path entry. `apps/web/src/routes/**` (a glob entry) does suppress.

## Hypotheses worth checking

1. Path-normalisation drift between the matcher and `Design.OrphanExport`'s file-key: the reporter prints `./apps/...` but the matcher may expect `apps/...` or vice versa. cd-no7 / cd-klp landed glob support — the exact-path code path may have regressed.
2. Default-export vs named-export divergence: `App.tsx` exports default; `glicko.ts` has named exports. Both fire, so this is unlikely the cause, but worth ruling out explicitly.
3. The matcher's exact-string compare may be doing `==` on the entry vs the canonicalised abs path, while glob entries route through `globset` which handles relative/abs symmetrically.

## Acceptance

- [ ] An exact-path entry in `[public_api].exports` suppresses `Design.OrphanExport` on every export from that file.
- [ ] Regression test added to `crates/cofferdam-engine/tests/spec_contract/public-api-orphans/` covering both `apps/foo.ts` and `apps/dir/**` entries on the same fixture.
- [ ] Real-repo validation against the bestefforttools layout (which doesn't currently hit this) confirms no new false positives.
- [ ] Verified against the user's reproducer: their poker-puzzle layout no longer needs `baseline write` for `App.tsx` / `index.ts` / `glicko.ts`.

## Related

- gh #41
- Built on cd-no7 (glob support in `[public_api].exports`) and cd-klp (re-export edges in `Design.OrphanExport` reachability)
- Reporter repo (private): `C:\Users\tajdi\poker-puzzle`
close_reason: resolve_public_api now absolutizes project_root via std::path::absolute before exact/glob key derivation, matching cd-q9f's source-path absolutize on the file_key side. Three regression tests pin a relative project_root + absolute file_key path through both exact and glob branches.

title: Design.OrphanExport flags exports imported via tsconfig paths (@/*) as orphan
description:
From GitHub issue #32 (https://github.com/TAJD/cofferdam/issues/32).

Adjacent to #27 but a distinct case. In a Next.js project where tsconfig.json declares 'paths': { '@/*': ['./*'] }, direct imports through the alias are NOT followed by Design.OrphanExport. Every export imported via @/lib/... or @/components/... is reported orphan, no barrel involved.

In a real repo (cofferdam 0.3.1) this dominates orphan-export count: ~30 of ~40 baselined Design.OrphanExport entries on components/*.tsx and lib/*.ts are this shape.

REPRO:
- tsconfig.json: { 'paths': { '@/*': ['./*'] } }
- lib/useFoo.ts: export function useFoo() { return 1 }
- components/Bar.tsx: import { useFoo } from '@/lib/useFoo'

Expected: 0 OrphanExport findings on useFoo.
Actual: useFoo is reported as orphan.

Relative-path import ('../../lib/useFoo') is followed correctly. The bug is alias resolution.

WHAT TRIED:
- [public_api].exports suppresses (workaround) — one entry per file across dozens.

SUGGESTED FIX:
Resolver should consult tsconfig.json compilerOptions.paths and baseUrl when computing the import graph for Design.OrphanExport. Next.js, Vite, and most modern TS setups configure @/* by default.

Related: #27 (barrel re-exports — same symptom, resolver-layer cause vs. public_api propagation).

Touches the import resolver in the engine; likely cofferdam-engine and Design.OrphanExport in cofferdam-checks/src/design.rs.
close_reason: Engine.analyze_with_sources promotes input paths to absolute via std::path::absolute, fixing TsconfigDiscovery::Auto walk + path_key mismatch. Verified: cargo test/clippy/fmt all clean, dedicated regression test in cofferdam-cli/tests/orphan_tsconfig_paths.rs covers the CWD-relative invocation. Real-repo spot-check on bestefforttools: relative + absolute invocations now agree.

title: Plugin findings are silently excluded from default check output, baseline writes, and the CI gate
description:
From GitHub issue #31 (https://github.com/TAJD/cofferdam/issues/31).

Findings emitted by external plugins (loaded via cofferdam.toml plugins = [...]) appear in 'cofferdam check --no-baseline --format=json' BUT are silently dropped from default 'cofferdam check' output, never appear in .cofferdam/baseline.json, and don't count toward --fail-on. Custom checks can't enforce anything in CI — defeats the plugin SDK's purpose.

REPRO:
1. Author plugin (e.g. Project.UseApiErrorHelper) that fires on at least one file.
2. Wire into cofferdam.toml: plugins = ['./tools/cofferdam-checks/api-error-helper']
3. cofferdam doctor → green
4. cofferdam check --no-baseline --format=json | jq '.findings[] | select(.id == "Project.UseApiErrorHelper")' → 3 findings
5. cofferdam check (default) → ZERO Project.UseApiErrorHelper findings; same exit code as pre-plugin
6. Inspect .cofferdam/baseline.json after baseline write → ZERO plugin entries; built-in entries written normally
7. cofferdam check --fail-on=medium → gate unaffected by plugin findings

EXPECTED:
Plugin findings should be first-class peers of built-in findings:
- Default check should print them
- --fail-on=<severity> should respect plugin findings' defaultSeverity
- Baseline writes should record plugin findings
- cofferdam-ignore directives should match plugin check ids

WHY IT MATTERS:
SDK README markets project-specific architectural rules as the use case. Right now custom checks are advisory-only via --no-baseline; can't gate merges, can't be baselined for incremental adoption, can't be silenced via inline directives.

SUGGESTED FIX:
Treat plugin findings the same as built-in throughout pipeline:
1. Include plugin-emitted findings in printed-findings stream and baseline-diff set
2. Flush plugin findings to .cofferdam/baseline.json
3. --fail-on ranges across both
4. cofferdam-ignore directives match against plugin check ids

If advisory-only is deliberate (plugin-side panic concerns), document AND provide opt-in: plugins.gate = true or per-plugin enforce = true.

Touches cofferdam-cli/src/main.rs::Cmd::Check, baseline write path, fail-on logic, and the suppression matcher.

title: Warning.TripleEquals fires on idiomatic == null / != null
description:
From GitHub issue #28 (https://github.com/TAJD/cofferdam/issues/28).

Warning.TripleEquals flags 'x == null' / 'x != null' as violations and recommends ===. But x == null is the standard JS/TS shorthand for 'x is null OR undefined' — replacing with === changes behavior (=== null no longer matches undefined). ESLint's eqeqeq has a 'smart' / 'always-except-null' option for exactly this reason; cofferdam has no equivalent.

REAL-WORLD IMPACT:
On the reporter's project, ALL 19 TripleEquals findings are == null / != null. 100% false positive rate. Only sensible action is to baseline forever, silently accepting any future real == bug.

Sample false positives:
- ./app/api/hyroxgeneric/route.ts:17 — if (config.exerciseCount == null)
- ./lib/searchParamReader.ts:12 — if (raw == null) return undefined
- ./lib/setupLink.ts:99,111,114 — same shape

SUGGESTED FIX:
Special-case null literal operands. Exempt:
- x == null, x != null
- null == x, null != x

All other ==/!= still flagged. Matches ESLint eqeqeq 'smart' semantics.

Optional: option flag allow_null = true (default true) so users wanting strict eqeqeq:always can opt in.

Touches crates/cofferdam-checks/src/warning.rs::TripleEquals.

title: Design.OrphanExport doesn't follow barrel re-exports; public_api.exports doesn't suppress them either
description:
From GitHub issue #27 (https://github.com/TAJD/cofferdam/issues/27).

In a Next.js + shadcn/ui project on cofferdam 0.3.0, Design.OrphanExport flags ~77 of 250 findings on barrel re-export sites: every symbol in components/ui/dialog.tsx is re-exported by components/ui/index.ts, which IS imported elsewhere. Cofferdam still reports the underlying file's exports as orphan. Adding the source file (or barrel) to [public_api].exports does not change the count.

REPRO:
- components/ui/dialog.tsx: export { Dialog, ... }
- components/ui/index.ts: export { Dialog, ... } from './dialog'
- import { Dialog } from '@/components/ui' elsewhere
- 10 OrphanExport findings on dialog.tsx, 0 on index.ts

WORKAROUNDS TRIED (all failed):
- Adding the barrel to [public_api].exports
- Adding each shadcn primitive file explicitly to exports
- Glob pattern 'components/ui/**.tsx'

SUGGESTED FIXES:
1. Follow re-export edges in OrphanExport reachability — if index.ts exports { X } from './foo', treat X in foo as reachable from index.ts. (Right fix.)
2. Make [public_api].exports actually suppress OrphanExport for listed files, with glob support. (Affordable workaround.)

Related: #32 (tsconfig paths not followed), #29 (UnusedSuppression on barrel directives).

title: Plugin findings are silently excluded from default check output, baseline writes, and the CI gate
description:
Mirrors GitHub issue #31: https://github.com/TAJD/cofferdam/issues/31

SUMMARY
Findings emitted by external plugins (loaded via cofferdam.toml's plugins = [...]) appear in 'cofferdam check --no-baseline --format=json' output, but are silently dropped from default 'cofferdam check' output, never appear in .cofferdam/baseline.json, and don't count toward --fail-on gating. Custom checks are effectively unable to enforce anything in CI — exactly the use case the plugin SDK exists to enable.

REPRO (cofferdam@0.3.0, check-sdk@0.3.0)
1. Author a minimal plugin that fires reliably on at least one file (reporter's repro: Project.UseApiErrorHelper flags inline NextResponse.json({error:...},{status:>=400}) in app/api/**/route.ts).
2. Wire it into cofferdam.toml: plugins = ["./tools/cofferdam-checks/api-error-helper"]
3. cofferdam doctor → green, plugin loads.
4. cofferdam check --no-baseline --format=json | jq '.findings[] | select(.id == "Project.UseApiErrorHelper")' → 3 findings reported.
5. cofferdam check (default, baseline-aware) — outputs ZERO Project.UseApiErrorHelper findings. Same exit code as before plugin existed.
6. .cofferdam/baseline.json after baseline op — ZERO Project.UseApiErrorHelper entries. Built-in check entries written normally.
7. Run with --fail-on=medium — gate is unaffected by the 3 plugin findings.

EXPECTED (plugin findings should be first-class peers)
- Default cofferdam check should print them alongside built-in findings.
- --fail-on=<severity> should respect plugin findings' defaultSeverity.
- Baseline writes should record plugin findings so existing tech debt can be baselined.
- Suppression directives (// cofferdam-ignore: <PluginCheckId>) should work on plugin findings.

WHY THIS MATTERS
SDK README markets project-specific architectural rules as the use case ('project-specific architectural rules as checks the same engine runs alongside the built-ins'). Right now, custom checks act only as advisory diagnostics surfaced via --no-baseline. They can't gate merges, can't be baselined for incremental adoption, can't be silenced via inline directives. The plugin system ships, but the integration is plumbed only one direction.

REAL-WORLD IMPACT
Reporter wrote Project.UseApiErrorHelper to codify a CLAUDE.md-documented rule. Fires on 3 noncompliant call sites correctly. But: new regressions won't fail any CI gate, existing noncompliance can't be baselined and gradually paid down, lint-staged pre-commit hook won't surface findings. Same shape applies to the existing Refactor.HyroxRng plugin in the same repo — defeats the rule-of-three example in the README.

SUGGESTED FIX
Treat plugin findings the same as built-in findings throughout the pipeline:
1. In the code path constructing the printed-findings stream and the baseline-diff set, include plugin-emitted findings.
2. baseline write must flush plugin findings to .cofferdam/baseline.json.
3. --fail-on must range across both built-in and plugin findings.
4. cofferdam-ignore directives must match against plugin check ids.

If plugin findings are intentionally advisory-only (e.g. concern about plugin-side panics destabilising the gate), at minimum document it AND add a config flag (plugins.gate = true or per-plugin enforce = true) to opt in.

INVESTIGATION POINTERS
- The plugin host runs in cofferdam-cli (run_plugins / run_plugins_with_sources). It returns plugin findings as Issues.
- The merge point with engine findings exists for the JSON robot output (since #6 issue confirms plugin findings appear in --no-baseline --format=json) but apparently NOT for: default text output, baseline write, baseline diff, --fail-on, suppression filter.
- Probable code paths to audit: crates/cofferdam-cli/src/main.rs (Cmd::Check assembly), the baseline-write code path, the --fail-on gate evaluation, suppression filtering.

ENVIRONMENT
- @cofferdam/cofferdam@0.3.0, @cofferdam/check-sdk@0.3.0
- Node 22.20.0, pnpm 10, Windows 11
- Next.js 16 + React 19

RELATED
#27 (orphan-export through barrels), #28 (TripleEquals on == null), #29 (UnusedSuppression false positive), #30 (NoConsoleLog scope mismatch). All filed in the same investigation pass.
notes:
Wire plugin findings through the full pipeline:

1. crates/cofferdam-cli/src/main.rs — added run_plugins_filtered helper and a sister run_plugins_filtered_with_signatures helper that applies inline-suppression directives to plugin findings and computes baseline signatures from the on-disk source. The baseline-aware check path, the no-baseline check path, and run_baseline_write all call the appropriate helper, so plugin findings now flow through default text output, the --fail-on gate, baseline writes, and baseline-tagging.

2. crates/cofferdam-formatters/src/text.rs — added an Other rendering bucket for findings whose check_id prefix is not one of the five built-in categories. Without this, plugin IDs like Project.UseApiErrorHelper were counted in the trailing summary but silently dropped from the per-category sections — same user-visible failure mode as the original bug.

Tests: crates/cofferdam-cli/tests/plugin_findings.rs covers (a) plugin finding in default text output, (b) --fail-on gate respects plugin severity, (c) baseline write records plugin findings, (d) once baselined, the same finding does not re-trigger the gate. Each test no-ops when Node is absent (CI runners without Node don't fail). Added a unit test in text.rs for the Other bucket.

Verification: cargo build / cargo test --workspace (400 passing, +5 from main) / cargo clippy -D warnings / cargo fmt -- --check all clean. Real-repo spot-check on gistreact corpus shows no regressions.
close_reason: Plugin findings now flow through default text output, baseline writes, the --fail-on gate, and inline-suppression filtering. Verified via integration tests + cargo test/clippy/fmt and a real-repo spot-check on gistreact.

title: Warning.TripleEquals fires on idiomatic == null / != null
description:
Mirrors GitHub issue #28: https://github.com/TAJD/cofferdam/issues/28

SUMMARY
Warning.TripleEquals flags == null / != null and recommends === / !==. But x == null is the standard JS/TS shorthand for 'x is null OR undefined' — replacing it with x === null *changes behavior* because === null no longer matches undefined. The full equivalent is x === null || x === undefined, which is verbose and almost never what people want at the call site.

ESLint's eqeqeq rule has a 'smart' (a.k.a. 'always-except-null') option that explicitly exempts comparisons against null for exactly this reason. cofferdam's check has no equivalent.

REPRO
  if (config.value == null) { ... }   // intentional null-or-undefined check
  if (raw != null) { ... }
cofferdam check — both fire Warning.TripleEquals.

IMPACT
On the reporter's repo: Warning.TripleEquals reports 19 findings; ALL 19 are == null / != null. Zero are real == vs === bugs. 100% false-positive rate on this codebase, so the only sensible action is to baseline it forever — silently accepting any future *real* == bug in those files. Defeats the purpose of the check.

Sample false positives (all idiomatic):
- ./app/api/hyroxgeneric/route.ts:17 — if (config.exerciseCount == null)
- ./lib/hyroxWodSetupLink.ts:34-38, 69-81 — URLSearchParams reader, if (param != null) out.x = param
- ./lib/searchParamReader.ts:12 — if (raw == null) return undefined
- ./lib/setupLink.ts:99, 111, 114 — same shape

FIX
Special-case null literal operands. Concretely, exempt:
- x == null, x != null
- null == x, null != x
All other == / != still flagged. Matches ESLint's eqeqeq: ['error', 'smart'] which the JS ecosystem has converged on.

Optional: option flag allow_null = true (default true) so users can opt in to strict eqeqeq: always.

ENVIRONMENT
- @cofferdam/cofferdam@0.3.0, @cofferdam/check-sdk@0.3.0
- Node 22.20.0, Windows 11

title: Design.OrphanExport doesn't follow barrel re-exports; public_api.exports doesn't suppress them
description:
Mirrors GitHub issue #27: https://github.com/TAJD/cofferdam/issues/27

SUMMARY
On a real Next.js + shadcn/ui repo running cofferdam 0.3.0, Design.OrphanExport flags symbols that are clearly reachable: every symbol exported by components/ui/dialog.tsx is re-exported by the barrel components/ui/index.ts, which is itself imported by app code. Cofferdam still reports all 10 as orphan. Adding the source file (or its barrel) to [public_api].exports in cofferdam.invariants.toml does not change the count.

REPRO
- components/ui/dialog.tsx exports the standard shadcn Dialog symbols.
- components/ui/index.ts re-exports them: export { Dialog, ... } from './dialog'
- App code imports via: import { Dialog } from '@/components/ui'
- pnpm exec cofferdam check --no-baseline --format=json reports 10 Design.OrphanExport findings on dialog.tsx and 0 on index.ts.

WHAT WAS TRIED
1. Barrel listed in [public_api].exports — index.ts itself is exempt (0 findings) but exemption doesn't propagate to files it re-exports from.
2. Each shadcn primitive added explicitly to [public_api].exports — count unchanged.
3. Glob 'components/ui/**.tsx' — no change; unclear whether globs are supported.

IMPACT
On the reporter's repo: 250 / 621 total findings are Design.OrphanExport, 77 of those come from this single shape. The check is genuinely useful but produces a flood of false positives on barrel patterns (shadcn, vendored UI libs, public SDK packages).

FIX OPTIONS (either resolves)
1. Follow re-export edges in Design.OrphanExport reachability. If index.ts imports Dialog from './dialog', dialog.tsx's Dialog is reachable from index.ts. (Right fix.)
2. Make [public_api].exports actually suppress Design.OrphanExport for the listed files, with glob support. (Cheaper workaround.)

DOCS GAP
The 'No package.json main/module/exports allowlist yet' limitation in docs/invariants/ is the same shape but the barrel re-export gap is not called out. Document it as a known limitation with the recommended workaround at minimum.

ENVIRONMENT
- @cofferdam/cofferdam@0.3.0, @cofferdam/check-sdk@0.3.0
- Node 22.20.0, pnpm 10, Windows 11
- Next.js 16 / React 19 / shadcn/ui

RELATED
Probably interacts with #29 (UnusedSuppression) — same shadcn-barrel pattern, different bug surface.
close_reason: Implemented glob support in [public_api].exports via PublicApi struct (exact HashSet + globset.GlobSet). Documented in docs/invariants.md. Verified: build, test (382 pass), clippy, fmt. Deeper fix (re-export edge in reachability) tracked separately as cd-klp.

title: cofferdam advise omits plugin checks from a file's Constraints list (gh #21)
description:
GitHub: https://github.com/TAJD/cofferdam/issues/21

`cofferdam advise <file>` lists every built-in check that applies to a file but omits plugin checks declared via `defineCheck` and registered in `cofferdam.toml`'s `plugins = [...]`, even when their FileScope would match.

Breaks the agent-advisory contract: advise is documented as 'an LLM agent shells out before editing a file, gets back per-rule constraints, and adjusts its plan before writing code'. Plugin checks are exactly the project-specific rules advise should help most with.

Fix: enumerate registered plugin checks the same way as built-ins, sourcing from Check.id, Check.category, Check.defaultSeverity, Check.explanation. Apply the same FileScope filter advise already applies to Design.LayerViolation etc.

Probably shares a root cause with gh #20 (pathPattern not filtering at runtime). Fix consistently with whatever the runtime filter ends up doing.
close_reason: (see individual bead notes)

title: FileScope.pathPattern parsed but doesn't filter at runtime (gh #20)
description:
GitHub: https://github.com/TAJD/cofferdam/issues/20

`defineCheck.files.pathPattern` is documented as 'when set, the file path must match' — but in 0.2.2 the engine invokes `run()` on files that don't match the pattern.

Repro: plugin scopes `pathPattern: "lib/{hyrox*,geneticAlgorithm}.ts"`, `cofferdam check --no-baseline` reports findings on `lib/seededRng.ts`, `lib/workoutHistory.ts` (don't match brace pattern). Confirmed via `cofferdam advise lib/seededRng.ts` — advise correctly knows the plugin doesn't apply (so the parser knows the pattern), but `check` invokes the plugin anyway.

Hypotheses (in order of likelihood):
1. pathPattern parsed but never applied to the discovery walker.
2. Brace expansion not honored by the globset matcher used here.
3. Path passed to globset has a different shape (absolute vs relative, leading `./`).

Breaks the plugin perf model: every plugin runs on every TS file. Forces authors to redo path filtering inside `run()`. Likely shared root with gh #21 (advise omits plugin checks).
close_reason: (see individual bead notes)

title: init --baseline writes broken .gitignore (gh #4)
description:
GitHub: https://github.com/TAJD/cofferdam/issues/4

`cofferdam init --baseline` scaffolds:
```
.cofferdam/
!.cofferdam/baseline.json
```
Per gitignore spec, you cannot un-ignore a file inside an excluded directory. Result: `baseline.json` is invisible to `git status` / `git add`, users commit without it, CI re-runs without baseline and fails on every pre-existing finding.

Fix: change scaffold to `.cofferdam/*` so the negation reaches the file. Add a CLI smoke test that `git check-ignore` reports baseline.json as non-ignored after `init --baseline` in a fresh repo.

Source: `cofferdam-cli` init scaffolding.

title: Severity axis + --fail-on=<level> CI gate
description:
Today: any finding → exit 1. Real adoption needs severity to be configurable per-check and gated separately from priority (priority sorts the report; severity gates CI).

Acceptance:
- Add Severity enum to cofferdam-core (Info, Low, Medium, High, Critical). Each CheckMeta gets a default_severity; cofferdam.toml can override per-check.
- New CLI flag --fail-on=<info|low|medium|high|critical> (default: medium for now). Exit 1 only when at least one finding ≥ threshold.
- Severity surfaced in text and JSON formatters.
- Defaults: Warning.* = High, Refactor.* = Medium, Design.* = Medium, Readability.* = Low, Consistency.* = Low. Tuned later, fine for v1.
- Compatible with baselines: baselined findings never trigger fail-on regardless of severity.

Design note: priority (computed, sorts) and severity (configured, gates) MUST stay separate axes per the README. Don't collapse them. Severity overrides live in [checks.X.Y] severity = 'high' in cofferdam.toml — depends on cd-4ms landing first.
close_reason: cd-t1a done; commit 327785f

title: Baseline workflow: cofferdam baseline write/check + --baseline + default fail-on-new
description:
Single biggest adoption unlock. New subcommand 'cofferdam baseline write' snapshots current findings to .cofferdam/baseline.json. 'cofferdam check' auto-detects the baseline file and defaults to --fail-on-new (only NEW findings produce exit code 1; baselined findings still print as 'baselined' but don't fail CI). Override with --no-baseline or --baseline=<path>.

Acceptance:
- Hash key per finding: (relative_path, check_id, rule_signature) where rule_signature is a check-defined stable hash of the matched code (NOT line number — line numbers churn on every reformat). Default rule_signature = SHA-256 of the trimmed offending span text.
- 'cofferdam baseline write' is idempotent and pretty-prints JSON with stable key order so diffs are reviewable.
- Schema versioned: {version: 1, findings: [...]}.
- Smoke test: write baseline on bestefforttools (~396 findings), re-run check, expect exit 0 and 'N findings (all baselined)' summary line.
- Add an unbaselined finding (edit any source file), expect exit 1 and only that finding in the report.
- JSON output gains a 'baselined' boolean per finding so robot consumers can filter.

Design note: rule_signature is the load-bearing decision. Line-number-based baselines invalidate on any reformat and become useless. Span-text-hash works but is fragile to whitespace; trim aggressively. Per-check override of rule_signature lets future checks (e.g. CognitiveComplexity) hash the AST shape rather than text.

Out of scope here: severity gating, --since (separate sub-issues under epic cd-g4y).
close_reason: Implemented baseline write/check workflow. SHA-256-of-trimmed-span signatures; schema versioned at v1; sorted entries; auto-detects .cofferdam/baseline.json; --baseline/--no-baseline/--fail-on-new flags; JSON gets baselined per-finding + summary.new/baselined. Validated end-to-end on bestefforttools (398 findings). Commit d0c9f73.

title: Stopgap npm wrapper (postinstall binary download)
description:
Phase 4 (cd-napi epic) ships @cofferdam/node via napi-rs prebuilt binaries — that's weeks of work. Meanwhile we want TS users to type `pnpm add -D cofferdam` and have it work TODAY.

Approach: thin npm package whose postinstall hook downloads the matching GitHub Release binary. Pattern used by esbuild (early), wasm-pack, biome (early days), etc.

Steps:
1. Create packages/cofferdam/ with a minimal package.json + scripts/postinstall.js
2. postinstall detects platform/arch (process.platform + process.arch), maps to a release artifact URL, downloads + extracts to node_modules/.bin/cofferdam
3. Bin entry in package.json so `pnpm exec cofferdam` resolves
4. CI: publish to npm on tag push (alongside the existing release.yml)
5. Document in README: `pnpm add -D cofferdam` then `pnpm exec cofferdam check src/`

Phase 4 will replace this with the napi-rs path transparently — same package name, users don't notice. The postinstall approach has known issues (corporate proxies, offline CI, sandboxed npm installs) that the napi-rs prebuilt approach solves; until phase 4 lands, this is the bridge.

Acceptance:
- Tom can `pnpm add -D cofferdam` in rovikore-landing-page and run `pnpm exec cofferdam check src/` without any other setup
- Works on macOS, Linux, Windows (x64 minimum; arm64 if release matrix produces it)
- postinstall failure has a clear error message pointing to the manual install path

title: Distribute cofferdam binary releases (pre-npm)
description:
Cut binary releases NOW so the user can pin cofferdam in their own repos before phase 4's full napi-rs npm publish lands. Enables real-world iteration via dogfooding.

Distribution paths:
1. **GitHub Releases**: tag-triggered, multi-platform binaries from the existing release.yml matrix (Linux x64/arm64 gnu+musl, macOS x64/arm64, Windows x64/arm64). Users `curl | tar` or download. — closest to today's tooling.
2. **cargo install**: `cargo install --git https://github.com/cofferdam/cofferdam cofferdam-cli` — Rust users, works today without any release infra.
3. **homebrew-cofferdam tap**: `brew install cofferdam/tap/cofferdam` — macOS dev experience.
4. **Scoop bucket** (Windows): user already uses scoop heavily.

Phase 4 will replace #1-#3 with the full `@cofferdam/node` npm distribution (the platform-specific binaries via napi-rs prebuilt artifacts). Until then:

Acceptance:
- `v0.0.2` tagged + GH Release published with at minimum linux-x64, mac-arm64, windows-x64 binaries
- Release workflow flips from `if: false` to gated on tag pushes (matches napi-rs template's pattern)
- Install-once instructions in README for each platform
- User can run `cofferdam check` in rovikore-landing-page and one other repo without local clone

Out of scope: npm publish, crates.io publish, Linux distros. Phase 4 / phase 6 territory.

title: Robot mode — AI-first JSON output
description:
Token-economical structured output for AI agents (Claude Code, Cursor, aider, etc.).

Flags:
- `--robot` / `--json` — machine-readable output, stable schema, no ANSI, no banner, no totals line
- `--robot --format=toon` — token-optimized format (1.6x more efficient than JSON for repeated keys)
- `--robot-meta` — include cursor + token-budget metadata for paginated runs

Schema (initial draft):
```json
{
  "findings": [
    {
      "id": "Warning.TripleEquals",
      "category": "warning",
      "priority": 15,
      "severity": "warning",
      "file": "src/foo.ts",
      "line": 42,
      "column": 8,
      "endLine": 42,
      "endColumn": 10,
      "message": "Use === instead of ==",
      "fix": null
    }

}
```

- Schema documented + JSON Schema artifact at `schemas/findings.schema.json` for tooling
- Token cost on a 200-finding run ≤ 30% of the text formatter's

title: baseline rule_signature drifts under whitespace-only reformat — pre-commit chain rejects valid commits
description:
From GitHub issue #33 (https://github.com/TAJD/cofferdam/issues/33).

When 'cofferdam baseline write' runs and is followed by a whitespace-only edit (e.g. prettier --write), the same logical findings re-emerge as NEW (un-baselined) on next 'cofferdam check'. Painful with husky + lint-staged: 'refresh baseline → git add → git commit' trips the pre-commit gate because lint-staged runs prettier inside the hook.

REPRO:
lint-staged config:
'*.{ts,tsx}': ['eslint --fix', 'prettier --write', 'cofferdam check --quiet --max-issues=20']

1. Edit TS file shifting baselined finding's location (add an import line)
2. cofferdam baseline write — succeeds, 'delta vs prior: 0' (logically nothing changed)
3. git add foo.tsx .cofferdam/baseline.json && git commit
4. lint-staged runs prettier --write on staged TS file; whitespace shifts marginally (1-line drift)
5. cofferdam check runs against prettier-formatted state, reports previously-baselined findings as un-baselined, fails commit

CONCRETE NUMBERS:
- After baseline write: Refactor.LongAndComplex showed [baselined] on line 165
- After in-hook prettier: same finding on line 166, no [baselined], blocks commit
- Workaround: prettier --write FIRST, THEN baseline write, THEN add and commit

SURPRISE:
Docs describe rule_signature as content-derived (so finding survives line moves). Empirically signature also depends on something that changes under whitespace reformat — possibly column position, exact slice fed into hash, or surrounding tokens prettier touches.

SUGGESTED FIX (preference order):
1. Make rule_signature invariant under whitespace-only reformat. Hash AST or normalized form (or symbol identity) instead of source slice.
2. Document lint-staged ordering pitfall (prettier → baseline write → check).
3. Optional 'cofferdam baseline reconcile' subcommand — re-sign baseline entries against current source without changing accepted set.

Related: #25 (baseline write delta reporting), #11 (--hide-baselined).

Touches the rule_signature hashing logic in cofferdam-engine and baseline persistence.
close_reason: signature_for_span now collapses internal whitespace runs; baseline schema bumped V1→V2 with a clear regen message on V1 load. Tests cover prettier-shape invariance + CRLF + token-boundary regression. End-to-end repro confirmed: edit file → baseline write → prettier-style reformat → check shows [baselined].

title: Warning.NoConsoleLog flags console.error and console.warn despite the name
description:
From GitHub issue #30 (https://github.com/TAJD/cofferdam/issues/30).

The check named Warning.NoConsoleLog fires on console.log, console.warn, AND console.error. The id implies log-specific scope, but the matcher is broad. Error message (e.g. 'remove console.error call') only reveals scope after the finding fires.

The three methods have different conventions:
- console.log — usually debug noise, fair to flag
- console.warn — often legitimate runtime warnings (deprecation, recoverable state)
- console.error — frequently the documented error-logging shape inside catch blocks

Treating all three identically produces high FP rate.

REAL-WORLD IMPACT:
On reporter's project, 15 findings: 13 console.error in catch blocks, 1 console.warn for recoverable case, 1 console.log gated behind NODE_ENV === 'development'. None should actually be removed. >90% FP rate.

SUGGESTED FIXES (preference order):
1. Split into Warning.NoConsoleLog, Warning.NoConsoleWarn, Warning.NoConsoleError (separate severities, opt-in/out per check). Matches ESLint no-console 'allow' option.
2. Rename to Warning.NoConsole with options methods = ['log', 'warn', 'error']. At least the name no longer lies.
3. Keep current check, exempt console.error inside catch blocks by default.

Touches crates/cofferdam-checks/src/warning.rs::NoConsoleLog and cofferdam-checks/src/lib.rs registration.

title: Schema versioning for invariants.toml, canonical graph, and DSL
description:
## Why

The invariants spec format is the public interface between projects and cofferdam. The canonical graph (cd-T1) is the public interface between adapters and rules. The predicate DSL (cd-9hp.1) is the public interface for project-authored rules. All three will evolve.

The Glean and Kythe experiences are unambiguous: **schema evolution without explicit versioning produces years of compatibility pain.** Without versioning, every engine release risks silently re-interpreting a long-lived spec or rule file in a way the project did not consent to.

We need to commit, **before the predicate DSL ships v1**, to a versioning discipline that survives the next decade. Doing this now is cheap (a `schema_version = 1` field is a one-line addition); doing it later is a coordinated migration across every project that adopted cofferdam.

## What

Three distinct schemas to version:

1. **`cofferdam.invariants.toml`** — the project-architecture spec.
2. **The canonical graph schema** (cd-T1) — emitted by adapters, consumed by rules.
3. **The predicate DSL** (cd-9hp.1) — surface syntax for scripted rules.

For each:

- Add an explicit `schema_version` field at load time.
- Engine refuses unknown future versions with a clear, actionable migration message ("this spec declares schema_version=3; this cofferdam build supports up to schema_version=2; upgrade cofferdam or pin to a previous version").
- Past versions are supported within a documented deprecation window (recommendation: N=3 minor releases for MINOR bumps, N=2 major releases for MAJOR bumps).
- Past versions outside the deprecation window are rejected with a "this cofferdam build no longer supports schema_version=1; please run `cofferdam invariants migrate` against cofferdam ≤ 0.5" message.

Versioning policy:

- `MAJOR.MINOR`, semver-flavoured.
- Additive changes (new optional fields, new node/edge types, new DSL predicates) bump MINOR.
- Breaking changes (removed fields, changed semantics, renamed predicates) bump MAJOR with a deprecation window.
- A `cofferdam invariants migrate` command (or documented manual recipe) for each MAJOR bump.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Versioning policy documented in `docs/schema-versioning.md`. Covers all three schemas.
- [ ] `schema_version` field plumbed for invariants.toml; missing field treated as v1 with a one-time deprecation hint at first run.
- [ ] `schema_version` field plumbed for the canonical graph schema (delivered alongside cd-T1).
- [ ] `schema_version` field plumbed for the DSL surface (delivered alongside cd-9hp.1).
- [ ] Tests cover: refused future versions, accepted past versions within deprecation window, rejected past versions outside it.
- [ ] All existing spec fixtures updated to declare version 1 explicitly.
- [ ] CHANGELOG section template includes "Schema changes" for every release; the release process gate fails if a schema-touching commit doesn't update the relevant version.

## Sequencing

The invariants.toml half can ship immediately and independently — it's a one-field change. The canonical-graph half ships with cd-T1. The DSL half ships with cd-9hp.1. Coordinating: this bead is the **policy** and the test harness; the per-schema implementations are owned by their respective beads.

**Priority: must land before cd-9hp.1 ships v1**, so the DSL goes out into the wild with a version field on day one rather than retrofitted after.
close_reason: schema_version field plumbed for cofferdam.invariants.toml with full validation matrix (MalformedSchemaVersion / FutureSchemaVersion / UnsupportedSchemaVersion); pure validate_version exercised across all four VersionCheck arms in unit tests; engine surfaces deprecation + missing-field hints; docs/schema-versioning.md captures the MAJOR.MINOR + deprecation-window policy that canonical-graph (cd-T1) and DSL (cd-9hp.1) will inherit; all spec fixtures updated to declare 1.0. Verified end-to-end with workspace tests and CLI smoke.

title: Canonical graph schema as the substrate for cross-file rules
description:
## Why

The corpus today (`crates/cofferdam-core/src/corpus.rs`) is a flat namespace of typed slots. The project's import/export graph lives implicitly across two well-known slots in `crates/cofferdam-core/src/graph.rs` (`IMPORTS`, `EXPORTS`); graph-aware checks (`Design.OrphanExport`, `Design.LayerViolation`, `Design.ImportCycle`, `Design.DeadExport`) reconstruct queries by joining those tables in their `finalize` body.

This shape works for the current built-in checks but cannot support:

- **Transitive-closure predicates** ("X transitively imports Y") needed by the predicate DSL (`cd-9hp.1`).
- **Edge-typed traversal** (imports-as-type vs imports-as-value, default-export vs named-export).
- **Domain-extension namespaces** (`sql.column`, `iac.resource`, `gql.field`) needed for non-TS adapters (`cd-9hp.<adapter beads>`).
- **Incremental analysis** (`cd-9hp.4`) — flat tables are hard to incrementalise; a graph store with explicit per-file fact provenance is the natural unit.

Reference precedents: Code Property Graphs (Yamaguchi et al., 2014), Glean's Angle schema, Kythe's node/edge taxonomy. See `docs/design-principles.md` §4 and `docs/cofferdam-architectural-review.pdf` §4 for the full lineage.

## What

- Design a **canonical graph schema** with a small core (file, symbol, declaration, import, export, layer-membership) and a **registered-extension mechanism**: adapters declare additional node/edge types under a namespace (`ts.*`, `sql.*`, `iac.*`).
- Pick a **storage strategy**. Decision criterion: query throughput on a 5k-file fixture, plus complexity of incremental update. Recommended order of evaluation:
  1. **Crepe** (in-process Rust Datalog) — simplest, no external dependency, type-checked rules.
  2. **Ascent** — similar to Crepe, slightly different ergonomics.
  3. **Embedded Soufflé** via `souffle-rs` — most powerful, brings a build-time dependency.
  4. **Custom in-memory triple store** — only if (1)–(3) prove unworkable.
- **Versioned schema**: `schema_version` field on the schema artifact (depends on `cd-T11`); engine refuses unknown versions with a migration message.
- **Backward-compat path**: the existing `IMPORTS` and `EXPORTS` corpus slots stay populated for as long as built-in checks reference them; adapters write to both slots and the new graph until built-ins migrate.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Schema design recorded as an ADR under `docs/decisions/<n>-canonical-graph-schema.md`. ADR covers: core node/edge taxonomy, attribute conventions, identity rules, extension mechanism, schema-versioning contract.
- [ ] New module (`cofferdam-graph` or in `cofferdam-core::graph`) exposing the canonical graph as a typed Rust API.
- [ ] At least one built-in check migrated from flat-table joins to graph queries; behaviour unchanged on existing fixture suite. Recommendation: `Design.OrphanExport` (current logic is the cleanest cross-file).
- [ ] Benchmark on `bestefforttools` (325 TS files): build cost and query cost compared against the flat-table baseline; regression budget recorded.
- [ ] `schema_version` plumbed; loading a future-version graph emits a clear error pointing at the cofferdam version that supports it.
- [ ] Predicate DSL (`cd-9hp.1`) v1 surface designed with this schema in mind; v2 of the DSL compiles against the graph backend without breaking v1 rule files.

## Sequencing

This is the **substrate** of cofferdam's v2 architecture. Independent of `cd-9hp.1` v1 (the DSL ships first against the flat-table shape), but required before the DSL can express transitive-closure or edge-typed predicates. The canonical-schema decision blocks `cd-T3` (adapter contract).
design:
## Two strategic calls, not one

This bead is foundational — the schema we ship pins how every future adapter (SQL migrations, IaC manifests, GraphQL schemas) describes its world. Two questions need your sign-off before code.

### Decision 1: storage backend

| Option | Build cost (5k files, estimated) | Query throughput | Ergonomics | Risk |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Crepe** (in-process Datalog macro) | ~2-3s | ~ms per query for typical predicates | rules in Rust; strict typing | Crepe is a one-author project; bus-factor concern. Active in 2025 but small ecosystem |
| **Ascent** | ~2-3s | similar to Crepe | similar; some folks prefer the syntax | similar bus-factor concerns |
| **Embedded Soufflé** (`souffle-rs`) | ~5-10s build cost (Soufflé compiles rules to C++) | fastest for complex Datalog | most powerful; rules in `.dl` files, not Rust | Soufflé is a binary build-time dep; CI complexity; deployment story uncertain |
| **Custom triple store** (HashMap-of-HashMaps with explicit transitive-closure caching) | ~1s | depends on indexing; ms for direct edges, can be slow for closure | full control; no third-party trust | rolling our own query optimiser is years of work if predicates grow |
| **petgraph + indexed attribute maps** (not in the bead, but worth comparing) | ~1s | direct-edge fast; closure expensive | well-known crate, idiomatic Rust | not Datalog; rule expression is imperative |

**Recommendation: petgraph + indexed attribute maps for v1, with the DSL evaluator owning closure caching.**

Why not Crepe / Ascent: Datalog elegance is real but our actual query workload — "does file F transitively import module M?", "which exports from layer L are reachable from layer K?" — is best served by typed graph traversal with attribute indexes. A Datalog engine is the right tool when the rule set is open-ended and large; ours is the predicate DSL's compiled output, which we control.

Why not Soufflé: build-time C++ dependency on every cofferdam install is an enormous cost. Worth paying when rule-set complexity demands it, not now.

Why not custom: petgraph already gives us a battle-tested directed graph; we layer attribute indexing on top.

If the predicate DSL grows enough that ad-hoc traversal stops scaling, we re-evaluate. The schema (decision 2) is the part that's hard to migrate; the backend is comparatively easy to swap.

### Decision 2: schema taxonomy

Two flavours of "small core + open extension" exist; they have different implications for adapter authors.

**(a) Closed core taxonomy, namespaced extensions**

```rust
enum NodeKind {
    File,
    Symbol,         // Class, Function, Variable, Type, Interface
    Declaration,    // The defining site of a symbol
    Import,
    Export,
    Layer,
    Extension { namespace: SmolStr, kind: SmolStr },
}

enum EdgeKind {
    DeclaredIn,     // Symbol → File
    Imports,
    Exports,
    BelongsToLayer,
    ImportsAsType,
    ImportsAsValue,
    Extension { namespace: SmolStr, kind: SmolStr },
}
```

Built-ins use the closed core; adapters use `Extension`. Predicate DSL switch-cases on core kinds and looks up `Extension` by `(ns, kind)` string match.

**(b) Open string-keyed taxonomy**

```rust
struct Node { kind: SmolStr, attrs: HashMap<SmolStr, Value> }
struct Edge { kind: SmolStr, attrs: HashMap<SmolStr, Value> }
```

Every node/edge is a string. Built-ins use convention (`"file"`, `"symbol.function"`, `"imports.as_value"`). No exhaustive Rust matches.

**Recommendation: (a) closed core, namespaced extensions.**

Closed core gives us exhaustive `match` ergonomics on the built-in path — every built-in check compiles against a known set of kinds, additions are caught at compile time, the JSON/SARIF schema is bounded. Extensions are namespaced and carried via `Extension { ns, kind }`; adapters declare their kinds in a registration file the engine reads at load.

Reference precedent: Code Property Graphs (Yamaguchi 2014) use this shape; Glean's Angle is even more strict (typed schema upfront). Kythe is the open-string counter-example and pays for it with looser tooling.

### v1 core schema — concrete proposal

```rust
// Nodes
pub enum NodeKind {
    File { path: PathBuf, lang: SmolStr },
    Symbol { name: SmolStr, kind: SymbolKind },
    Import { specifier: SmolStr },
    Export { name: SmolStr },
    Layer { name: SmolStr },
    Extension { ns: SmolStr, kind: SmolStr, attrs: AttrMap },
}

pub enum SymbolKind { Function, Class, Interface, Type, Variable, Namespace, Other }

// Edges
pub enum EdgeKind {
    DeclaredIn,        // Symbol → File
    ImportsAsValue,    // File → File (via Import)
    ImportsAsType,     // File → File
    ExportsAs { kind: ExportKind },  // File → Symbol or File → File (re-export)
    BelongsToLayer,    // File → Layer
    Extension { ns: SmolStr, kind: SmolStr, attrs: AttrMap },
}

pub enum ExportKind { Named, Default, ReExport }
```

`AttrMap` is `BTreeMap<SmolStr, Value>` where `Value = String | i64 | bool | List<Value>`. JSON-roundtrippable. Adapters store domain-specific facts in attrs (e.g. SQL migration's statement index, IaC resource type).

Identity: nodes get a stable `NodeId = u64` from a HashBuilder hash of `(NodeKind discriminant, identifying attrs)`. Edges are addressed by `(source_id, target_id, kind discriminant, kind-specific attrs)` — multiple edges between the same two nodes are allowed when their kind differs.

### What this unblocks

- **cd-9hp.1**: DSL v2 compiles graph queries against this surface. v1 grammar reserves the syntactic room.
- **cd-9hp.10**: adapter contract — adapters populate this graph via a registered `Adapter` trait. Each adapter's namespace is the only thing that varies.
- **cd-9hp.4**: incremental analysis — per-file provenance on every Node/Edge gives us natural invalidation units.

### What it doesn't decide

Storage backend (decision 1 above). The graph **API** is stable across petgraph / Datalog / custom backend; we pick petgraph for v1 and leave the door open.

### Acceptance

- [ ] ADR under `docs/decisions/<n>-canonical-graph-schema.md` covers: core taxonomy, identity scheme, attribute conventions, extension mechanism, versioning contract (inherits cd-9hp.12's `schema_version` policy).
- [ ] `cofferdam-graph` crate (or `cofferdam-core::graph`) exposes the typed Rust API.
- [ ] `Design.OrphanExport` migrated from flat-table joins to graph queries; spec_contract fixtures unchanged.
- [ ] Benchmark on `bestefforttools` (325 TS files): graph build cost ≤ 1.5× the current flat-table baseline; regression budget recorded.
- [ ] `schema_version` plumbed.
- [ ] cd-9hp.1's v1 grammar designed against this schema (no compatibility break on v2 graph promotion).

### Effort

10-15 days end to end. This is the largest single piece in the epic after cd-9hp.4. Sequenced:

1. ADR + core type definitions (2 days).
2. petgraph backend + attribute indexing (2-3 days).
3. Migrate `Design.OrphanExport` (1-2 days).
4. Benchmark + regression analysis (1 day).
5. Schema versioning wiring (1 day).
6. Spec_contract fixtures + docs (1-2 days).
7. Buffer (2-3 days).

### What I need from you

- Sign-off on **petgraph + indexed attributes** (decision 1). Override candidates: Crepe if you want declarative rules; Soufflé only if you have a use case I'm missing.
- Sign-off on **closed core + namespaced extensions** (decision 2). This is the harder-to-migrate call.
- Optionally: spawn a fresh bead for `cd-9hp.9.1` (storage spike) to validate decision 1 before committing to the full schema work. Recommended if you want a load-bearing data point before the 10-15-day commitment.

Holding open until both decisions land. cd-9hp.1 v1 work can proceed against the flat-corpus shape in parallel; v2 lift onto this graph happens after both ship.

title: action-smoke workflow hits 403 on unauthenticated GitHub API call for latest release tag
description:
SUMMARY
.github/workflows/action-smoke.yml resolves the 'latest' cofferdam release by curling https://api.github.com/repos/TAJD/cofferdam/releases/latest with no auth headers. Anonymous calls share a low rate-limit pool with every other unauthenticated runner on the GitHub-hosted fleet, so the call intermittently returns HTTP 403 and the workflow fails before it ever exercises the cofferdam-check action.

REPRO
Latest occurrence: workflow run 25453227871 on commit ea1c4c5 (main, 2026-05-06).
Log line: 'curl: (22) The requested URL returned error: 403'.
Prior run on 41ff0ed succeeded — confirms it's flaky, not a structural break.

EXPECTED
The release-resolution step should authenticate with the workflow's own GITHUB_TOKEN so it gets the per-installation rate-limit budget instead of the shared anonymous pool.

SUGGESTED FIX
In the curl invocation under .github/actions/cofferdam-check/ (or wherever 'version: latest' is resolved), add:
  -H "Authorization: Bearer ${{ github.token }}"
GITHUB_TOKEN is available by default in workflows; no extra permission grant needed for public release reads.

WHY THIS MATTERS
Random red CI on main blocks the 'main is always green' invariant and trains us to ignore the action-smoke status. Cheap, one-line fix.

RELATED
Surfaced while investigating CI status after cd-1c7 landed.
close_reason: Added GITHUB_TOKEN auth header to release-lookup curl in action.yml. One-line fix; no test surface since this only affects rate-limit behaviour on GitHub-hosted runners.

title: Spec contract: end-to-end fixtures pinning invariants.toml interpretation
description:
## Why

`cofferdam.invariants.toml` is supposed to be a contract: declare architectural intent, the engine emits findings against it. Today the only round-trip test is in `crates/cofferdam-core/src/invariants.rs:452`, which proves "parse → serialise → parse" stability. There is no end-to-end test of the form *"given THIS spec on THIS fixture, the engine emits EXACTLY these findings."* If a refactor changes the interpretation of layers, frozen boundaries, or invariants, we won't catch it until a downstream user does.

## What

Build a fixture matrix at `tests/spec-contract/` (or under `crates/cofferdam-engine/tests/`):

```
tests/spec-contract/
  layers-allowlist/
    cofferdam.invariants.toml
    src/...           # deliberately violates and respects layer rules
    expected.json     # canonical findings
  frozen-boundary/
    ...
  public-api-orphans/
    ...
  forbid-imports/
    ...
  combo-multi-rule/
    ...
```

CI runs each fixture, compares engine output to `expected.json`, fails on diff. Provide a `--update` mode for intentional regenerations (keeping a `git diff` step in PR review honest).

## Acceptance

- [ ] At least 5 fixtures spanning layers, frozen boundaries, public_api, forbid/require, and a multi-rule combo.
- [ ] CI gate; a deliberate one-line tweak to invariants.rs fails the relevant fixture.
- [ ] Documented as the canonical place to add a fixture when shipping new spec semantics.

Cheap insurance; small payoff per fixture, large payoff over the lifetime of the spec.
close_reason: Landed: 6 spec-contract fixtures (layers-allowlist, frozen-boundary, public-api-orphans, forbid-imports, require-imports, combo-multi-rule) + tests/spec_contract.rs runner. Each fixture pins the engine's exact findings via expected.json. Bless workflow: BLESS_SPEC_CONTRACT=1 cargo test -p cofferdam-engine spec_contract. Drift detection verified — flipping one word in design.rs::BoundaryFrozen's message format failed spec_contract_frozen_boundary. CI runs them through 'cargo test --workspace'. Documented as the canonical place for new spec-semantic fixtures in the module doc comment.

title: Incremental analysis: file-hash cache + finalize replay
description:
## Why

Every `cofferdam check` run reparses every file from scratch. The `cofferdam-lsp` crate is a stub. Daemon mode, IDE integration, and "quick feedback in CI on changed files only" all depend on an incremental analysis pipeline.

## What

- Per-file content hash → cache `(parse, per-file findings)`.
- Corpus snapshot keyed by the union of file hashes that contributed to each slot.
- On change: replay only affected files; recompute corpus slots whose contributors changed; re-run finalize.
- Preserve corpus typing (`CorpusKey<T>`) across runs — serialisation contract for slots, or in-memory daemon-only first.
- Modes: `--watch` (daemon), `--since <ref>` (CI), LSP push.

## Acceptance

- [ ] `cofferdam --watch` mode that re-emits findings on file change without full reparse.
- [ ] No-op re-run is at least 10× faster than cold run on a 300-file repo (e.g. `bestefforttools`).
- [ ] Corpus correctness pinned by a multi-file fixture test: edit one of N files contributing to a corpus slot, verify finalize sees the new aggregate.
- [ ] LSP crate gains a real (non-stub) handler that uses the incremental engine.

Likely the biggest engineering project in the epic.
design:
## Decision points — three calls, all consequential

This is the largest single piece in the epic per the bead. Three architectural calls overlap; all three need your sign-off before code, and the work itself is best decomposed into checkpoints that each ship independently.

### Decision 1: cache storage tier — memory-only vs disk-backed

| Option | Re-run latency (300 files, warm) | Cold start | Daemon-mode? | CI mode? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **In-memory only** (daemon process holds cache) | ~ms | ~3s (parse + analyze) | yes, native | no — `cofferdam check` from cold every time |
| **Disk-backed** (sled or CBOR-on-disk + content-hash keys) | ~100ms (deserialise + check) | ~3s + cache write | yes | yes — `cofferdam check --since HEAD` reads disk cache |
| **Hybrid** (in-memory for daemon; disk for one-shot CI) | best of both | ~3s | yes | yes |

**Recommendation: hybrid (in-memory daemon + disk cache for one-shot).** The acceptance gates "no-op re-run ≥10× faster" — achievable either way for daemon, but the `--since <ref>` CI use case can't work without disk. Cost: one serialisation contract for cached slots (CBOR or postcard), plus a cache-eviction policy.

### Decision 2: cache key — content-hash only vs (content-hash, config-hash, engine-version)

A check's output depends on three things: the file's content, the cofferdam.toml + invariants.toml config (and thus the resolved options), and the engine version (a check upgrade might emit different findings on the same input).

| Option | Risk | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| **Content-hash only** | Stale findings when config or engine changes | cheapest |
| **Per-(content, config, engine) hash** | Correct; cache invalidates on config change | one more hash field per entry |
| Content-hash + version-pin baked into cache directory name | Equivalent to (b) but blunt — every engine upgrade nukes the cache | acceptable for daemon, ugly for CI |

**Recommendation: per-(content, config, engine) hash.** Cofferdam's hot path is a few hash computations; we're not pinching nanoseconds. The correctness story matters more.

### Decision 3: corpus snapshot strategy — slot-level vs check-level

The corpus accumulates state across per-file `run()` calls and is read by `finalize()`. For incremental analysis, when one of N files contributing to a slot changes, we need to either (a) re-aggregate just that slot's contribution from the changed file, or (b) re-run the check entirely on every file. (a) is much faster but requires the slot to support **incremental updates**.

| Option | Re-run cost | Slot author complexity |
|---|---|---|
| **Replay-affected-files** (current corpus, no incremental updates) | O(files changed × checks) for per-file pass; full finalize | low; existing corpus stays unchanged |
| **Incremental slot updates** (slot author provides `remove_contributions_from(file)`) | O(files changed × checks) for per-file pass; finalize sees pre-removed-and-re-added view | high; every slot author updates contracts |
| **Hybrid** (default: replay-affected-files; opt-in incremental for hot slots like IMPORTS/EXPORTS) | best of both for the common case | low for new slots, high for hot built-in slots |

**Recommendation: hybrid — start with replay-affected-files for all slots, add incremental updates to hot built-in slots (IMPORTS, EXPORTS, layer-membership) in a follow-up.** First-checkpoint scope is "replay-affected-files works correctly"; the speed-up over cold run depends on per-file `run()` being the dominant cost, which it is on TypeScript.

Hot-slot incremental updates are a separate ~3-day piece per slot; defer until benchmarks show the replay-only path is the bottleneck.

### Multi-checkpoint plan

This is the right shape for a multi-day project per the prompt: checkpoints that each ship a working subsystem behind a flag.

**Checkpoint 1: content-hash cache for parse trees, in-memory only (~3 days)**

- New `cofferdam_engine::cache` module with a content-hash → ParsedView cache.
- `Engine.analyze_with_text` consults the cache before parsing; cache populated on miss.
- Daemon mode behind `--watch` (file-watcher via `notify` crate; invalidate on file change).
- No corpus snapshot yet — corpus rebuilt from scratch every cycle.
- Acceptance: no-op re-run ≥3× faster (parse is the dominant cost; subsequent checkpoints get us to 10×).

**Checkpoint 2: per-file findings cache (~3 days)**

- Cache (content-hash, config-hash, engine-version) → `Vec<Issue>` per file per check.
- Skip per-file `run()` when cache hit AND file's contributions to corpus don't matter (i.e. when `meta().consistency == false` and the check doesn't write to corpus).
- Acceptance: no-op re-run ≥7× faster.

**Checkpoint 3: corpus snapshot + replay-affected-files (~4 days)**

- Serialise corpus slots after every run (CBOR via the corpus key's `T: Serialize`).
- On next run: identify changed files (content-hash diff against last run); replay only their per-file `run()`; re-aggregate affected slots; re-run finalize.
- Acceptance: no-op re-run ≥10× faster on the 300-file fixture. Corpus correctness fixture pins multi-file slot semantics.

**Checkpoint 4: disk-backed cache + `--since <ref>` (~2 days)**

- Disk cache at `.cofferdam/cache/` (gitignored, configurable path).
- `cofferdam check --since <git-ref>` reads disk cache, runs only changed-files-relative-to-ref.
- Acceptance: CI usage shaves ~70% off cold-run time on `bestefforttools`.

**Checkpoint 5: LSP integration (~3-4 days)**

- `cofferdam-lsp` crate gains a real handler.
- LSP push events drive cache invalidation.
- VS Code extension exercise (smoke test, not shipped).
- Acceptance: editor shows findings on file save within ~500ms.

Each checkpoint ships behind no flag (additive, no behavioural change for users who don't opt in). `--watch` and `--since <ref>` are opt-in CLI surfaces.

### Total effort

15-20 days end to end, plus contingency. The biggest piece in the epic and worth treating as a small project, not a single bead.

### What I need from you

- Sign-off on **hybrid cache** (decision 1). The alternative is in-memory only with no `--since <ref>` CI path; I don't recommend it but it's a defensible scope cut.
- Sign-off on **(content, config, engine) hash key** (decision 2). The cheap alternative (content-only) is a foot-gun that will eventually waste your morning.
- Sign-off on **replay-affected-files for all slots, incremental opt-in later** (decision 3). The aggressive alternative (incremental from day one) inflates the timeline by ~50% with no payoff until benchmarks show the bottleneck.
- Optionally: collapse checkpoints 4 and 5 into separate beads (cd-9hp.4.4 and cd-9hp.4.5) and treat this bead as the first 3 checkpoints only.

The work I can sketch the v1 architecture for is bounded; the decisions above are not. Holding open.

title: ts-morph worker pool for requires_types checks
description:
## Why

`CheckMeta::requires_types` (`crates/cofferdam-core/src/check.rs:84`) is a declared flag intended to route type-aware checks to a ts-morph backend. The router does not exist, so no check can usefully set the flag. This blocks an entire class of valuable checks (unused-symbol detection across boundaries, type-narrowing assertions, branded-type misuse).

## What

- Spawn N ts-morph worker processes; design the IPC contract (request: file + node selectors; response: resolved type info / symbol info).
- Engine pre-routes checks declaring `requires_types = true` to the worker pool; results are folded back into the normal `Issue` stream.
- Decide whether plugins can declare `requires_types` (probably yes, eventually, but not v1).
- Worker-pool lifecycle: warm start, file-watch invalidation hooks (forward-compat with incremental analysis).

## Acceptance

- [ ] At least one type-aware built-in check ships using the router (candidate: `Warning.UnusedNullCheck` or a "narrowed-type-not-respected" check).
- [ ] CI smoke test exercises the worker pool on a non-trivial project.
- [ ] Worker startup cost is measured and documented; not paid when no type-aware check is enabled.
- [ ] `cofferdam.toml` opt-out for users who don't want the Node runtime overhead.
design:
## Decision points

Three architectural calls overlap in this bead. All three want your sign-off before code starts; the second is the only one with a clear default.

### 1. Worker runtime: ts-morph (Node) vs LSP-mode tsserver vs swc/oxc-type-extraction

| Option | What it gives us | Cost | Maturity |
|---|---|---|---|
| **ts-morph in Node worker** | Full TS Compiler API; resolves types, symbols, narrowed flow types | ~200MB / cold start ~3s / per-file ~50-200ms | mature, well-documented |
| **tsserver LSP client** | Same type info as ts-morph; tsserver is what VS Code uses; we'd speak the LSP JSON wire | ~200MB / cold ~2s / per-file ~20ms after warm-up (LSP caches) | mature but LSP integration is ours to maintain |
| **swc/oxc type extraction** (when shipped) | Native Rust, no Node runtime; partial coverage of the TS type system | ~0 startup; per-file fast | not yet shipped; oxc roadmap |

**Recommendation: ts-morph in Node worker.** Real type info, mature API, the cost (~200MB RAM) is acceptable for a code-quality tool. LSP-mode tsserver is more efficient but the wire protocol surface is large; ts-morph is one library API. Native Rust type-extraction is the long-term right answer but doesn't exist yet — we'd be writing the type system ourselves, which is years of work.

The flag-routing infrastructure we ship here works identically against any backend, so picking ts-morph for v1 doesn't lock us in.

### 2. IPC contract: stdin/stdout JSON-RPC vs napi-rs in-process vs ZeroMQ

| Option | Latency | Crash containment | Complexity |
|---|---|---|---|
| **stdin/stdout JSON-RPC** | ~1ms per call (newline-delimited JSON) | excellent — child crashes, parent reads EOF, respawn | low; we already use this for the plugin host |
| napi-rs in-process | ~0.1ms per call (FFI, no serialisation) | poor — Node crash takes down cofferdam | high; FFI lifetime management, build-time wiring |
| ZeroMQ / tcp socket | ~1ms per call | excellent | medium; needs port management |

**Default: stdin/stdout JSON-RPC.** Same pattern as `crates/cofferdam-cli/scripts/plugin-host.mjs` (cd-81a.7), which is battle-tested. The wire format is the IPC contract; bumping it follows the cd-9hp.12 versioning policy.

I'll proceed with this unless you flag it.

### 3. Plugin authoring: can plugin checks declare `requires_types: true` in v1?

The bead says "probably yes, eventually, but not v1". The reasons to keep it engine-only for v1:

- The plugin SDK's check shape (`packages/check-sdk/src/define-check.ts`) already exposes `requiresTypes: boolean` but the plugin host doesn't surface type info into `SourceFile`. We'd need a wire shape for resolved-type queries from the plugin's `run()`.
- That wire shape is non-trivial: plugin asks for "the type of node X", the engine routes to the worker, returns a serialisable type representation. Designing that round-trip is a separate bead.

**Recommendation: ship v1 engine-only.** Plugin support is cd-9hp.2.B, raised when a real plugin use case appears.

### Acceptance unchanged from the bead

- [ ] At least one type-aware built-in check ships using the router. Candidate: `Warning.UnusedNullCheck` — flags `if (x != null) {}` where x's TS type already excludes null.
- [ ] CI smoke test on a non-trivial project (suggestion: gistreact, which has enough TypeScript complexity to exercise narrowing).
- [ ] Worker startup cost measured and documented; not paid when no type-aware check is enabled (auto-opt-out: if no built-in check has `requires_types: true` AND `cofferdam.toml` doesn't enable a type-aware plugin, the worker pool isn't spawned at all).
- [ ] `cofferdam.toml` opt-out: `[engine] type_aware = false` to force-disable even when a type-aware check is registered (CI machines without Node runtime).

### Effort estimate

7-10 days end to end:

1. IPC wire schema spec + Node worker scaffold + cold-start measurement (2 days).
2. Engine routing (workspace-internal `requires_types` dispatch; results folded into Issue stream) (2-3 days).
3. `Warning.UnusedNullCheck` implementation (1-2 days).
4. CI smoke + opt-out wiring + docs (1-2 days).
5. Buffer (1-2 days).

### What I need from you

- Sign-off on ts-morph (decision 1). Worth a quick reality check: do you have a working ts-morph install on your dev box, or does CI need to install Node + npm-install ts-morph as part of the cofferdam install?
