Without these, this bead is the right place to stop and ask. Holding it open.

title: Embedded predicate DSL inside cofferdam.invariants.toml (top lever)
description:
## Why

`cofferdam.invariants.toml` is the strongest abstraction in the tool — one declarative file describes "what is this codebase supposed to be" and many checks interpret it (layers, frozen boundaries, public-API entry points, forbid/require imports). Today it covers about 80% of architectural rules.

The remaining 20% — "all controllers must have a registered test", "no calling X without holding lock Y", "components in `ui/` must not touch `localStorage`", data-flow constraints — need expressive predicates. Without them, projects fork the binary or write a JS plugin to encode local rules.

## What

Embed a small scripting layer inside `cofferdam.invariants.toml` so projects declare scripted predicates without compiling Rust or shipping a JS plugin. Sketch:

```toml
[invariants.scripted."controller-test-pair"]
when = "file matches 'src/controllers/**/*.ts'"
require = "exists 'tests/controllers/' + basename(file)"
message = "Every controller needs a registered test"
```

Pick an embedded language (Rhai, Starlark, CEL, or a custom mini-DSL) — small surface, deterministic, sandboxable. The scripted-rule runtime is one Rust check that walks the table at engine startup, compiles each rule, and dispatches over files (and corpus state in `finalize`).

## Acceptance

- [ ] Embedded scripting choice documented in a design note (decision record).
- [ ] `[invariants.scripted]` section parses, round-trips, and validates.
- [ ] At least 2 fixture rules: one file-level, one cross-file (uses corpus).
- [ ] Bad scripts fail fast at config load with a useful error, not at file 4000.
- [ ] `docs/invariants.md` documents the DSL surface end-to-end.
- [ ] Real-repo validation against `bestefforttools` and `gistreact` shows no regressions on existing rules.

This is the recommended highest-lever item in the architecture-extension epic.
design:
## Decision: custom mini-DSL (not Rhai / Starlark / CEL)

### The four candidates, ranked

| Option | Embedded crate | Sandbox | Type system | Stdlib footprint | DX for non-programmers |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Custom mini-DSL** | none (parser ~200 LOC) | total — only predicates we ship are callable | bool predicate, no expressions beyond comparison | minimal, deterministic | best — TOML-ish surface, no Turing-completeness to trip over |
| Rhai | `rhai` (~30k LOC, ~1.5MB binary growth) | partial — function allowlist + recursion limits, but Rhai is a real scripting language | dynamic, JS-like | large stdlib, mutable state, closures | familiar to JS authors but Turing-complete (unbounded loops, runtime errors at file 4000) |
| Starlark | `starlark-rust` (~50k LOC, ~3MB) | strong — frozen-at-load, no mutation outside scope, no I/O | typed-ish, Python-ish | Bazel-flavoured stdlib (lists, dicts, strings) | familiar to Bazel users only; not actually simple |
| CEL | `cel-rust` (~10k LOC, ~800KB) | strong — type-checked, no side effects, designed to be embedded | typed expressions | small | "Common Expression Language" — actually decent, but a single-expression model fights the `when/require/message` shape |

### Why custom mini-DSL

The bead's example sketch already shows what we actually need:

```toml
[invariants.scripted."controller-test-pair"]
when = "file matches 'src/controllers/**/*.ts'"
require = "exists 'tests/controllers/' + basename(file)"
message = "Every controller needs a registered test"
```

That surface is three string fields, each parsed against a small grammar:

- **`when` / `require`**: boolean predicates over a fixed vocabulary — `matches`, `exists`, `imports`, `layer`, `forbid`, `require`, `transitively`, plus a few literals (`file`, `basename(file)`, layer names, glob strings). Closed set; ~15 primitives ship in v1.
- **`message`**: format-string templating with `{file}`, `{layer}`, `{match}` substitutions.

A custom parser for this is a one-day Pratt-or-recursive-descent affair. The total grammar is smaller than `cofferdam.invariants.toml`'s own `[boundaries]` syntax.

The three real-language options all overshoot:

- **Rhai's** Turing-completeness is the wrong tool for a configuration file. A rule that infinite-loops is a configuration error, not a runtime behaviour. Worse: cd-9hp.4 (incremental analysis) wants to *cache* rule evaluation per file-hash — opaque scripting languages make that brittle. Predicate DSLs (CEL-style) make it trivial.
- **Starlark** has Bazel cachet but the grammar is bigger than our problem and it carries a frozen-at-load model that doesn't simplify suppression vs. a custom parser we control.
- **CEL** is the closest match technically (designed-for-embedding, declarative, fast) but `cel-rust` is less mature than the Go reference and the single-expression model forces us into `when && require` AND patterns rather than the natural separated `[when, require, message]` shape — that's a DX regression on the doc-readable surface, for no real win.

### v1 grammar pin (forward-compat with cd-9hp.9 graph promotion)

The grammar pins these surfaces from v1 so v2's graph substrate doesn't break existing rules:

- **Subject namespaces** (per the cd-9hp.1 notes update): `core.*`, `ts.*`, `_.*` (reserved for builtins), plus open registration for `sql.*`, `iac.*`, `gql.*`, etc. v1 only ships `core` and `ts` resolvers; unregistered namespaces error helpfully at config load.
- **Transitive operator**: `transitively imports`, `transitively reaches` — parsed in v1 but only the direct-edge case implemented (flat corpus). v2 graph promotion adds the closure.
- **Edge-typed traversal**: `imports as type Y` vs `imports as value Y` reserved in grammar.
- **Glob in subject**: `file matches '<glob>'` already in the sketch; reuse the same globset crate the boundaries section uses.

### What ships in v1

- `cofferdam_core::dsl` — Pratt parser (~300 LOC) + AST + evaluator over flat corpus (~500 LOC).
- One built-in check `Design.ScriptedInvariant` that walks `[invariants.scripted.*]`, compiles each rule at engine startup, fails fast on bad scripts.
- Two fixture rules in spec_contract: one file-level, one cross-file via `imports`.
- `docs/invariants.md` documents the v1 vocabulary; `docs/schema-versioning.md` adds the DSL row to the version policy table.
- `schema_version` in the DSL surface itself: every rule inherits the invariants.toml schema_version (1.0); future grammar bumps require MAJOR.

### Acceptance

- [ ] Custom mini-DSL parser + evaluator land under `cofferdam_core::dsl`.
- [ ] `[invariants.scripted]` section parses, round-trips, validates with actionable error messages on bad scripts.
- [ ] Two spec_contract fixtures: file-level rule + cross-file rule (uses `imports`).
- [ ] Bad scripts fail fast at config load (cofferdam refuses to start; error names the rule and line).
- [ ] `docs/invariants.md` documents the DSL vocabulary end-to-end.
- [ ] Real-repo validation against `bestefforttools` and `gistreact` shows no regressions.
- [ ] Grammar reserves multi-domain namespaces (`core.*`, `ts.*`, `_.*`, plus open `<ns>.*`) per the bead's forward-compat addition.

### Effort estimate

4-6 days end to end, sequenced as:

1. Grammar spec doc + Pratt parser tests (1 day).
2. AST + evaluator over flat corpus (1-2 days).
3. `Design.ScriptedInvariant` integration + spec_contract fixtures (1 day).
4. Real-repo validation + docs (1 day).
5. Buffer (1 day).

### What I need from you

Sign-off on the custom mini-DSL choice. If you want one of the off-the-shelf options instead, say which and I'll re-brief; I won't ship the parser blind. Most likely override would be CEL (closest technical match, mature crate) — say so if you've worked with `cel-rust` and have a reason to prefer it.
notes:
## Design lens: graph substrate + logic/language separation

The corpus today (`crates/cofferdam-core/src/corpus.rs`) is a flat typed-slot store; the project's import/export graph already lives across two well-known slots in `crates/cofferdam-core/src/graph.rs` (`IMPORTS`, `EXPORTS`). Existing graph-aware checks (`Design.OrphanExport`, `Design.LayerViolation`, `Design.ImportCycle`) reconstruct graph queries by joining those tables inside `finalize`.

Predicates like *"every controller transitively imports the audit module"* or *"no symbol exported from layer X is reachable from layer Y"* are awkward against flat `Vec<ImportRecord>`, natural against a queryable graph. The DSL is likely to converge on graph-shaped queries even if v1 doesn't need them. We will probably end up implementing some flavour of in-memory knowledge graph as the substrate; better to leave room for it now than to lock the DSL into table-only query semantics.

### Layered architecture (target shape, not v1 work)

This bead also frames the broader logic-vs-language separation:

1. **Domain adapter** — parser-specific code that populates a canonical typed graph. TS: oxc + `cofferdam-engine/src/graph.rs`. Future: GraphQL, SQL migrations, IaC manifests, schema files. The adapter's job is graph population, nothing else; rule logic does not appear here.
2. **Canonical graph schema** — domain-neutral node/edge types (file, symbol, declaration, import, layer-membership, span) extensible by adapters with their own variants (`sql.column`, `gql.field`, `iac.resource`). Node identity is stable across runs.
3. **Predicate DSL** — operates over the canonical graph; does not know the source language. Same surface for TS and SQL: `forbid edge(layer="app") -> node(kind="iac.resource") with attribute(public_ip=true)`.
4. **Domain-specific rules** — written in the DSL using domain-specific node/edge types contributed by an adapter. The rule lives close to the codebase it governs; the DSL surface is shared.
5. **Output** — already domain-neutral via `Issue` + `Span` + `RelatedSpan`. No work needed.

### Sequencing

- **v1 (this bead):** predicate DSL over the *current* flat-corpus shape. Gets ~80% of expressiveness without paying for graph-substrate engineering. Designed so v2 can lift the same DSL onto a graph backend without breaking surface syntax.
- **Later:** promote the project graph from "two well-known slots" to a first-class queryable subsystem (in-memory triple store / mini-Datalog / Cypher-flavoured layer). Migrate the DSL to graph queries. Keep `IMPORTS`/`EXPORTS` slots populated for backward compatibility with built-in checks.
- **Further still:** adapter contract for non-TS domains. Generic node/edge schema versioned independently from the engine. Plugin authors register adapters, not bespoke parsers.

### Risks of over-abstracting early

- **Premature schema commitment.** The graph schema could over-fit the "every domain looks like a code import graph" mental model. SQL migrations, IaC, and schema-IDL each pull in their own dominant relations; the canonical schema needs to stay open without becoming meaningless.
- **DX regression.** Pure graph queries are powerful but worse-DX than `function.parameters.length > 10`. The DSL needs sugar (or convention) for common per-file-shape predicates so users don't drop into Datalog for trivial rules.
- **Span semantics** assume text-source artifacts (byte offsets). Binary or generated artifacts (compiled IaC plans, machine-translated schemas) complicate this; not blocking, but a forcing function on the canonical schema.
- **Performance.** Graph-query optimisation is non-trivial; an in-memory naive evaluator is fine for ~500k-edge codebases but stops scaling well above that without indexes.

### Acceptance addendum

Beyond the original ACs, the v1 DSL design should explicitly reserve syntactic room for:

- [ ] Reachability / transitive-closure predicates ("X transitively imports Y").
- [ ] Edge-typed traversal ("X imports-as-type Y" vs "X imports-as-value Y").
- [ ] Domain-extension namespaces (so `sql.foreign_key` is a recognised predicate target without core-engine changes).

These don't have to be implemented in v1; they have to be *unblocked* by the surface choice, so v2 can ship without breaking v1 rules.
## Forward-compat addition (v1): multi-domain namespaces

The v1 DSL surface must accept **domain-extension namespaces** in predicate references — `sql.*`, `iac.*`, `gql.*`, etc. — even though no second-domain adapter ships in v1. The cost is approximately zero (a syntactic decision in the parser); the cost of NOT doing this is rewriting every existing v1 rule when the first non-TS adapter lands. Forward-compat is the whole point.

### Required syntactic acceptance from v1

- **Namespaced predicate references**: `sql.column.not_null`, `iac.resource.public_ip`, `core.import.from_layer` — parse to a `(namespace, predicate_path)` pair.
- **Namespace registration**: an adapter (cd-T3) declares the namespace it owns. Rules referencing an unknown namespace fail at config-load time with a clear error: `"no adapter registered for namespace 'sql' — predicate sql.column.not_null cannot be resolved"`.
- **Reserved namespaces**:
  - `core` — cofferdam built-ins; always present.
  - `ts` — TypeScript adapter (the existing pipeline once refactored under cd-T3).
  - `_` — the local project's ad-hoc namespace, for project-private predicates.

### v1 implementation scope

This is **purely forward-compatibility**. v1 implementation can stop at:

- Parser accepts namespaced syntax.
- Validator produces a useful error if the namespace isn't registered.
- A single namespace (`core` plus the implicit project namespace) is supported end-to-end.

Lookup wiring for non-core namespaces lands with cd-T1 (canonical graph schema) and cd-T3 (adapter contract). The v1 DSL's job is to not foreclose them.

### Why this can't wait

Adding namespacing to a DSL after rules exist in the wild requires either a breaking change (rename every existing predicate to `core.X`) or a permanently muddy syntax (`X` means `core.X` if no adapter, otherwise ambiguous). Both are bad. Doing it now is a one-evening change in the parser.

Cross-reference: see `cd-T11` for the schema-versioning policy that covers this.

title: Architecture extension surface: redeem the design pledges
description:
Cofferdam has a strong architectural backbone — declarative `CheckMeta`, three-phase `Check` contract (`run` / `pass2` / `finalize`), typed `CorpusKey<T>` shared state, and `cofferdam.invariants.toml` as a single architectural spec read by many checks. Several pledges are unredeemed or partial:

- **`requires_types: true` is a flag without a router** — no ts-morph worker pool exists, so type-aware checks block.
- **Configurable taxonomy is documented but not wired** — `Category` (`crates/cofferdam-core/src/check.rs:29`) is a closed enum, yet doc claims projects can add categories.
- **`observes_findings` has one user** — `Consistency.UnusedSuppression` is alone; the mechanism is real but barely exercised.
- **No incremental analysis** — every run reparses; `cofferdam-lsp` stays a stub.
- **`invariants.toml` is declarative but limited** — covers ~80% of architectural rules; data-flow / "X iff Y" predicates need an embedded scripting layer.
- **Corpus failure modes are hostile to plugins** — slot type-id mismatch panics; plugin authors can collide on names.
- **Plugin cross-file collaboration is unclear** — built-ins share state via `CorpusKey<T>` but the SDK surface for plugins doing the same is undocumented.
- **No spec → findings integration suite** — `invariants.toml` round-trips but is not pinned by end-to-end fixture tests.

This epic groups those open items so they can be triaged and sequenced together. The recommended top lever is **the embedded predicate DSL inside `invariants.toml`**, because it most amplifies the strongest part of the design (single shared spec, many interpreting checks) without forcing plugin authors to reach for Rust or JS.

Source: design retro on 2026-05-06; full prose lives in `docs/design-principles.md`.

title: Design.OrphanExport: follow re-export edges in reachability
description:
Follow-up to cd-no7 (the bounded glob-support fix) and the deeper half of GH #27 (https://github.com/TAJD/cofferdam/issues/27).

PROBLEM
Even with glob support in [public_api].exports (cd-no7), Design.OrphanExport's reachability graph does not follow re-export edges. If components/ui/index.ts re-exports Dialog from ./dialog and is imported by app code, dialog.tsx's Dialog should be reachable. Today it's reported as orphan unless the user explicitly listsdialog.tsx in [public_api].exports.

FIX
In crates/cofferdam-checks/src/design.rs::compute_orphans, treat 'export X from Y' edges the same as regular imports: when index.ts has 'export { Dialog } from ./dialog', record an import edge from index.ts to dialog.tsx for symbol Dialog. Then the existing reachability walk picks it up.

CONSIDER
- Shared with cofferdam-core/src/graph.rs if the import graph lives there.
- May need test fixtures mirroring the shadcn barrel pattern (one barrel index.ts + 2-3 primitive files).

DEPENDS ON
- cd-no7 (glob support) — ship that first to unblock the immediate user pain, then this.

OUT OF SCOPE
- Glob support in [public_api].exports — that's cd-no7.
- Documenting the limitation — handled in cd-no7 if it lands first.
notes: Investigation 2026-05-07: today's behavior already covers the simple shadcn-barrel case via the lenient reexport_sources HashSet (any file that's the resolved_source of any re-export is treated as if all its exports are namespace-touched). That heuristic is too lenient: a *dead* barrel still shields its primitives from being flagged. Plan: (1) remove the unconditional reexport_sources shortcut; rely on per-edge ImportRecord 'touched' set which the engine already populates for re-export edges (engine/graph.rs:343-374). (2) Fix default-via-Named-reexport edge case: when an ImportedName with kind=Named has source_name='default', map it into default_touched. (3) Add fixture orphan_export_barrel/ + unit tests covering: shadcn-barrel positive, dead-barrel negative, aliased re-export, default re-export. (4) Real-repo validation against bestefforttools + gistreact.
close_reason: Removed lenient reexport_sources shortcut; rely on engine's per-edge ImportRecord 'touched' set (set since cd-7h5). Added Named-source-name='default' → default_touched mapping for the export-default-from edge. Added 7 unit tests + orphan_export_barrel/ shadcn-style fixture. Real-repo finding sets unchanged on bestefforttools (30 orphans before/after, byte-identical). Live-set reachability filtering (dead barrel still shielding primitive via per-edge touch) acknowledged as out-of-scope and pinned in dead_barrel_no_longer_shields_primitive test.

title: Warning.NoConsoleLog flags console.error and console.warn despite the name
description:
Mirrors GitHub issue #30: https://github.com/TAJD/cofferdam/issues/30

SUMMARY
Warning.NoConsoleLog fires on console.log, console.warn, AND console.error calls. The id strongly implies it's specific to console.log (so users — and LLM agents reading the check id — reasonably expect a narrow scope), but the actual matcher is broad. The error message reveals the broad scope ('remove console.error call (use a logger or strip in CI)') only after the finding has fired.

The semantic mismatch matters because the three methods have very different conventions:
- console.log — almost always debug noise. Fair to flag.
- console.warn — often legitimate runtime warnings (deprecation, recoverable degenerate state).
- console.error — frequently the documented error-logging shape inside catch blocks, especially in Node, edge-rendered code, or any project without a structured logger.

Treating all three as 'the same thing to remove' produces a high false-positive rate and trains users to baseline / suppress without thinking — worst of both worlds.

REPRO
  try { await doThing() } catch (err) { console.error('doThing failed', err) }
Run cofferdam check — Warning.NoConsoleLog fires.

IMPACT
On the reporter's repo, Warning.NoConsoleLog reports 15 findings:
- 13 are console.error in catch blocks (API routes, localStorage access, image-export failures). All match the project's documented error-handling convention.
- 1 is console.warn for a recoverable degenerate case (no exercises matched a focus filter).
- 1 is console.log, gated behind if (process.env.NODE_ENV === 'development') — intentional dev-only debug helper.
None of the 15 should actually be removed. >90% false-positive rate on this codebase. As with #28, the only sensible action is to baseline the entire check forever, silently accepting any future *real* console.log that slips in.

FIX OPTIONS (in preference order)
1. Split into separate checks: Warning.NoConsoleLog, Warning.NoConsoleWarn, Warning.NoConsoleError. Default severities can differ (log medium; warn/error low or info). Users opt-in/out per-check. This is what ESLint's no-console plugin effectively offers via the allow option.
2. Rename to Warning.NoConsole with options methods = ['log', 'warn', 'error']. At least the name no longer lies about scope.
3. Keep the current check but exempt console.error inside catch blocks by default. AST-aware. Fixes the most common false positive without touching the API or the name.

(1) is cleanest and lines up with how other lint ecosystems handle this. (2) is the cheapest fix that removes the surprise.

BONUS
The current behavior also makes the auto-fix suggestion ('use a logger or strip in CI') harder to act on. console.error in a catch block is *already* a logger of last resort. 'Strip in CI' doesn't apply to error-handling paths. The advice fits console.log but not console.error — another argument for splitting.

ENVIRONMENT
- @cofferdam/cofferdam@0.3.0, @cofferdam/check-sdk@0.3.0
- Node 22.20.0, Windows 11

RELATED
#27 (OrphanExport / public_api), #28 (TripleEquals on == null), #29 (UnusedSuppression false positive). Same shape — checks that make sense in principle but produce dominantly-false-positive results on a real-world TS/Next.js codebase.
close_reason: Narrowed Warning.NoConsoleLog default to console.log only and added methods config (default ['log']) with options: ['log','warn','error','info','debug',...]. Rule id unchanged (no breakage). 8 new unit tests + fixture + doc. Verified: build, test (390 pass, +8), clippy, fmt. Commit on main.

title: Decide fate of the unscoped 'cofferdam' npm package (transfer / leave / unpublish)
description:
After the rename to @cofferdam/cofferdam in v0.2.3, the unscoped `cofferdam` package still exists on npm, still owned by user tajdickson at version 0.2.2. Three options:

1. **Deprecate-only** (covered by separate bead): leave ownership where it is, just emit redirect on install. Simplest. Cost: the @cofferdam org page on npm doesn't list the unscoped name, so the project's npm presence stays split.
2. **Transfer ownership to @cofferdam org**: matches the spirit of the original cd-0pq. Both names appear under the org page, both have the same maintainer set, no single-user dependency. Procedure: npmjs.com/package/cofferdam/access → add @cofferdam org as maintainer → remove tajdickson personal owner. Requires a paid org plan if the unscoped package was free-tier (verify).
3. **Unpublish**: only possible within 72 hours of the last publish (so likely already past the window for the existing 0.2.2 publish). Even if eligible, npm strongly discourages unpublishing user-facing packages.

ACCEPTANCE:
- Pick one of the three options.
- If 1 or 2: execute the chosen path, verify on npmjs.com.
- If 3 and outside the window: close as won't-fix.

CONTEXT: created when cd-0pq was superseded by the rename. Depends on the deprecate bead landing first so users get a redirect regardless of which option wins.
close_reason: Deprecation executed by user (Thomas) 2026-05-06; npm registry CDN propagation pending but the write has landed. cd-3b2 resolved as 'deprecate-only' option — the unscoped name stays owned by tajdickson personal account, with the migration message redirecting installs to @cofferdam/cofferdam. No ownership transfer needed.

title: Add Consistency.UnusedSuppression lint check (gh #26)
description:
GitHub: https://github.com/TAJD/cofferdam/issues/26

`docs/suppression.md` already calls this out as future work. Suppressions outlive their cause silently — the underlying check changes, the code changes, the file is deleted-and-recreated nearby — and there's no signal.

Check id: `Consistency.UnusedSuppression` (mirrors existing `Consistency.BroadSuppression`).

Fires when:
1. `// cofferdam-ignore: <CheckId>: ...` directive's targeted line has no current finding for `<CheckId>`.
2. `// cofferdam-ignore-start: <CheckId>` ... `-ignore-end` range contains no current findings.
3. `// cofferdam-ignore-file: <CheckId>` directive's file has no current findings (excluding the suppression itself).

Severity: low/info — almost always cleanup work, not bugs.

Edge case: when `<CheckId>` itself isn't loaded (plugin not installed, check renamed/removed), don't flag — that's a different lint (`Consistency.UnknownCheckId` if added later).

Implementation should be cheap — already track suppression locations during the suppression pass; comparison to findings is O(N) over the issue list. Surface in `cofferdam doctor` as warn-level discoverable counter even when check disabled.

title: Per-check pages don't indicate autofix support; no fix --dry-run (gh #24)
description:
GitHub: https://github.com/TAJD/cofferdam/issues/24

`cofferdam fix` claims to apply mechanical autofixes for 'supported checks' and silently skips the rest. Users can't predict which checks are supported without running fix and observing what changed.

Combined with gh #22 (TripleEquals autofix corrupts `== null`), this makes the whole subcommand feel risky to enable in CI / pre-commit.

Plan:
1. Add `autofix: bool` field to `CheckMeta`.
2. Per-check doc pages render an 'Autofix: yes/no' badge in their frontmatter table.
3. Catalog index (`docs/checks/index.md`) groups or notes autofix support.
4. `cofferdam explain <CheckId>` includes 'Autofix support: yes/no' in metadata.
5. `cofferdam fix --dry-run` lists IDs it WOULD touch (non-destructive preview).

(5) is the highest-leverage change: answers 'what will fix actually do here?' without modifying files. Pair with gh #22's resolution.

title: baseline write should prune entries now suppressed inline (gh #19)
description:
GitHub: https://github.com/TAJD/cofferdam/issues/19

Audit trap: a finding that's baselined today, then later receives an inline `// cofferdam-ignore: ...` directive. After the directive lands, the finding is suppressed at runtime, but the baseline still contains the entry. Removing the suppression months later doesn't restore 'this finding fails CI' — the baseline silently grandfathers it.

docs/suppression.md already warns that 'a finding that is both baselined and suppressed is an audit trap', but tooling doesn't actively help users avoid it.

Two paths:
1. `baseline write` prunes entries whose corresponding finding is now suppressed at the file/range/file-wide level. Show pruned entries in the rendered diff.
2. `cofferdam baseline lint` (or `doctor` check) reports dual-state entries: 'X at lib/y.ts:32 is in the baseline AND suppressed inline — remove one.'

title: Misleading TOML error when top-level key follows a [checks.X] table (gh #23)
description:
GitHub: https://github.com/TAJD/cofferdam/issues/23

If `cofferdam.toml` has a top-level key (e.g. `plugins = [...]`) AFTER one or more `[checks."..."]` tables, TOML's scoping nests it under the most recently opened table. Cofferdam's error then misleads:

`error: option validation failed for [checks."Readability.MaxFunctionLength"]: check does not declare option 'plugins'`

User wrote a structurally valid TOML file whose semantics happen to nest `plugins` under the wrong table.

Fixes (in order of leverage):
1. When validation fails because a known top-level key (`plugins`, `extends`, `include`) appears under `[checks."..."]`, emit a directive error explaining TOML scoping. Tell the user to move `plugins = [...]` to the top of the file.
2. Doc note in the configuration section about TOML scoping (cheapest, doesn't fix the runtime UX).

(1) is the right fix. New-adopter footgun: this is exactly the class of error a user hits in their first hour with the tool.
close_reason: added ConfigError::MisplacedTopLevelKey for plugins/extends/include nested under [checks.X] tables; emits a directive error explaining TOML scoping instead of the misleading 'check does not declare option' message. 4 unit tests.

title: pnpm exec cofferdam check JSON output polluted by SIGPIPE error (gh #13)
description:
GitHub: https://github.com/TAJD/cofferdam/issues/13

When `cofferdam check --format=json` is invoked through `pnpm exec` and the consumer closes the pipe early (`| head`, `| jq -e ... | head`), pnpm appends an error to stdout AFTER the JSON ends:

```
{ "findings": [...], "summary": {...} }
undefined
 ERR_PNPM_RECURSIVE_EXEC_FIRST_FAIL  Command "cofferdam" not found
```

Trailing string breaks downstream JSON consumers.

Likely cause: SIGPIPE / pnpm-recursive-exec interaction. pnpm wrapper detects broken pipe, treats as child failure.

Fix (cheapest): install a SIGPIPE handler in `bin/cofferdam.js` that exits cleanly. `process.on('SIGPIPE', () => process.exit(0))` or equivalent.

Alternative: doc that `pnpm exec cofferdam check` should redirect to a file for JSON consumption (`> findings.json`) — `npx cofferdam` doesn't show the issue. SIGPIPE handler in the shim is the leverage; doc note is the safety net.
close_reason: added SIGPIPE + stdout/stderr 'error' EPIPE handlers in bin/cofferdam.js so pnpm wrapper does not append undefined / ERR_PNPM_RECURSIVE_EXEC_FIRST_FAIL after JSON when consumer closes pipe. Additive 16-line change, no Rust impact.

title: MaxFunctionLength: skip blank/comment lines + add Refactor.LongAndComplex
description:
Two related changes:

1. `Readability.MaxFunctionLength` currently counts raw line span (`end_line - start_line`). Refactor to count effective lines: skip blank lines and pure-comment lines (any line whose trimmed text starts with `//`, `/*`, or `*` and is flagged `is_comment` by oxc).

2. New check `Refactor.LongAndComplex` — fires only when a function exceeds BOTH a length threshold (default 75 effective lines) AND a cyclomatic threshold (default 15). Higher-confidence refactor signal than either dimension alone. Severity High, base_priority 12.

Use existing `cofferdam_core::Lines` for line classification. Cyclomatic counting mirrors `Refactor.CyclomaticComplexity`'s visitor.

Files: `crates/cofferdam-checks/src/readability.rs`, `crates/cofferdam-checks/src/refactor.rs`, `crates/cofferdam-checks/src/lib.rs` (registration + shared helper), new `crates/cofferdam-checks/docs/Refactor.LongAndComplex.md`, new `examples/long_and_complex.ts`.

Verify with full block + run against `C:/Users/tajdi/bestefforttools` to confirm noise reduction on MaxFunctionLength and that LongAndComplex produces a sensible top-N.

title: Publish-time guard: check @cofferdam/check-sdk tarball includes dist/ (gh #10)
description:
GitHub: https://github.com/TAJD/cofferdam/issues/10

`@cofferdam/check-sdk@0.2.0` and `0.2.1` showed signs of an incomplete publish (dist files missing from tarball). package.json correctly lists `files: [dist, README.md, LICENSE]` and `main: dist/index.js` but those resolve to nothing if `pnpm build` hasn't run before `npm publish`.

Add to the SDK release workflow:
```yaml
- name: Verify SDK tarball contents before publish
  run: |
    cd packages/check-sdk
    npm pack --dry-run --json | jq -e '.[] | select(.files | map(.path) | index("dist/index.js"))' > /dev/null
```
Same pattern for `cofferdam` package guarding `bin/cofferdam.js`.

Also verify whether `prepublishOnly` already runs the build — if yes, this is belt-and-suspenders; if no, this is the actual fix.

A successful-but-empty publish is invisible from the publisher side and only catches when a downstream consumer fails to load the package. Cheap to gate.

title: Surface pnpm v10 hint when postinstall is silently blocked (gh #9)
description:
GitHub: https://github.com/TAJD/cofferdam/issues/9

pnpm v10's default sandbox blocks postinstall scripts unless the package is in `pnpm.onlyBuiltDependencies`. Without that, `pnpm add -D cofferdam` 'succeeds' but the Rust binary never downloads. `cofferdam --version` then fails with a hint pointing at `npm rebuild cofferdam` — wrong tool for pnpm projects.

Three fixes, ship together:
1. Detect pnpm in `scripts/postinstall.js` (via `process.env.npm_config_user_agent`) and emit a hint mentioning `pnpm.onlyBuiltDependencies` + `pnpm rebuild cofferdam`.
2. Update binary-not-found error message to suggest `pnpm rebuild cofferdam` if the calling environment looks pnpm-shaped.
3. README install section: add a 'pnpm users' callout.

(1)+(2) are the leverage; (3) is the safety net.
close_reason: cofferdam.js shim now detects pnpm/yarn/npm via lockfile + user-agent, prints package-manager-tailored recovery hint; postinstall.js prints the onlyBuiltDependencies fix when run under pnpm; README has a pnpm callout. Smoke-tested all three package managers.

title: Layer glob negation doesn't override alphabetical layer ordering (gh #5)
description:
GitHub: https://github.com/TAJD/cofferdam/issues/5

When two layers' globs overlap, the alphabetically-first layer wins, and gitignore-style negations within a single layer's glob list don't refine that. There's no documented way to say 'leaf layer wins specificity-wise' except renaming layers to sort first.

Repro (cofferdam 0.2.2):
```toml
[layers]
ui         = ["components/ui/**"]
components = ["components/**", "!components/ui/**"]
```
`cofferdam advise components/ui/button.tsx` reports Layer: components, expected ui.

`docs/checks/Design.LayerViolation.md` says 'place specific layer globs ahead of broad ones if they overlap', but ordering is alphabetical, not config-file order.

Design call needed:
1. Honor `!pattern` negations within a layer's glob list (intuitive; matches gitignore mental model).
2. Document the rename-to-sort workaround.

Recommend (1). Rename-as-priority is a leaky abstraction.

Decide approach before implementing.
design: Approved 2026-05-06. See design/cd-31r-layer-resolution.md. Two-part fix: (1) gitignore-style ! negations within a single layer's glob list; (2) cross-layer specificity = longest non-glob prefix in include patterns wins, alphabetical break ties. Files in scope: crates/cofferdam-core/src/layers.rs + Design.LayerViolation.md source + CHANGELOG.md. Controller runs gen-docs at merge.
close_reason: Layer matcher refactored to gitignore-style include/exclude pairs per layer + cross-layer specificity = longest non-glob prefix wins (alphabetical tie-break). Bead repro now resolves Layer: ui correctly. 6 unit tests + design doc landed at design/cd-31r-layer-resolution.md + CHANGELOG entry.

title: Consolidate npm publishing under the @cofferdam org
description:

title: cofferdam.invariants.toml — project-wide architectural spec
description:
Today architectural intent is encoded per-check (e.g., [layers] in cofferdam.toml is read only by Design.LayerViolation). This bead promotes that to a canonical project-wide spec — the artifact that answers 'what is this codebase supposed to be?' — readable by humans, agents, AND multiple checks at once.

This is the input 'cofferdam advise' (cd-lfx) reads to compute applicable constraints for a path. It's also a human-readable architecture document that doubles as machine-checked enforcement.

PROPOSED SCHEMA
[layers]
infra  = [\"src/infra/**\"]
domain = [\"src/domain/**\"]
app    = [\"src/app/**\"]

[layers.allow]
domain = [\"infra\"]
app    = [\"domain\", \"infra\"]

[public_api]
exports = [\"package.json:exports\", \"src/index.ts\"]
# OrphanExport check uses this to skip flagging items reachable from public_api

[boundaries]
\"src/legacy/**\" = { frozen = true, reason = \"see ADR-0007\" }
# A frozen boundary forbids new code; checks emit findings on additions.
# v0 may stub-warn on use without enforcing — full implementation gets its own bead.

[invariants]
\"no-direct-db-access\" = { forbid_imports = [\"src/infra/db\"], from_layers = [\"app\"] }
# Custom one-off invariants — like ad-hoc layer rules but more flexible.
# v0: support forbid_imports / require_imports primitives. Richer DSL future bead.

WHY THIS MATTERS
- One canonical artifact for architectural intent. Multiple checks read from it.
- New invariants can be added without writing a new check (when they fit the declarative shape).
- It's the input cofferdam advise reads to compute applicable constraints.
- It's the artifact a human reads to understand the codebase's architecture without reading every check config.
- It's the artifact an agent reads (or queries via advise) to know what NOT to do.

MIGRATION
- Existing [layers] config in cofferdam.toml continues to work — invariants.toml is additive. Document the precedence (invariants.toml wins when both present) and emit a deprecation hint when [layers] is found in cofferdam.toml.
- Public-API allowlist for OrphanExport gets factored out of any per-check config and into [public_api]. Update Design.OrphanExport to read here.

ACCEPTANCE
- 'cofferdam.invariants.toml' is a recognized config file alongside cofferdam.toml, with auto-discovery walking up from the cwd.
- Schema covers [layers], [layers.allow], [public_api], [boundaries], [invariants].
- Design.LayerViolation reads from invariants.toml in addition to cofferdam.toml's [layers] block (precedence: invariants > cofferdam.toml).
- Design.OrphanExport reads [public_api] for its allowlist; existing exemption logic continues to work when no spec is present.
- [boundaries] frozen=true is enforced for at least 'forbid new files matching the glob' — fuller semantics (forbid modifications) gated on a follow-up bead.
- [invariants] supports forbid_imports + require_imports primitives, evaluated as a generic Design.InvariantViolation check that fires per declared invariant.
- Doc page docs/invariants.md explains the schema with worked examples (mirroring the current cofferdam.toml docs).
- Round-trip test: load → re-serialize → load matches.

OUT OF SCOPE
- Full [boundaries] enforcement beyond 'forbid new files'. Modification-locking gated on a separate bead.
- Generative tooling ('cofferdam invariants suggest' that proposes layer rules from observed graph) — interesting but file separately.
- Cross-language portability of the spec. The schema is not language-specific in design, but TS-only matters today.

No hard blockers. Can run in parallel with cd-lfx; cd-lfx benefits when this lands but does not require it.

title: cofferdam advise <path> — JIT architectural advisory for agents
description:
New CLI subcommand that takes a path (file, directory, or glob) and emits, in robot mode, the rules and constraints that APPLY to that path — independent of whether any current code violates them. The point is to give an agent the architectural envelope of a file BEFORE it edits it, not after.

This is the load-bearing primitive of the cofferdam-as-context-substrate epic. Agents have cold-start context; they cannot read CLAUDE.md every session. 'advise' lets them query exactly what they need to know about the file they're about to touch, in a form that's idiomatic for tool use (one shell-out, JSON back).

OUTPUT (robot-mode, line-delim JSON; --format text for humans)
For each path:
- Layer membership (when [layers] is configured)
- Applicable rule set (filtered by file extension and any per-rule scope/exclude config)
- Per-rule rationale snippet (same source as 'cofferdam explain <id>')
- Per-rule parameters relevant to this file (e.g., MaxLineLength's limit)
- Public-API status (whether this file is reachable from the public_api allowlist — feeds OrphanExport exemption logic)
- Referenced invariants from cofferdam.invariants.toml when that lands (cd-???)

Sketch:
{
  \"path\": \"src/domain/user.ts\",
  \"layer\": \"domain\",
  \"public_api\": false,
  \"constraints\": [
    {\"rule\": \"Design.LayerViolation\", \"applies\": \"imports must target [infra, domain]\",
     \"forbidden\": [\"app\"], \"rationale\": \"...\"},
    {\"rule\": \"Design.OrphanExport\", \"applies\": \"all exports must be imported in-project\",
     \"exempt\": false, \"rationale\": \"...\"},
    {\"rule\": \"Refactor.CyclomaticComplexity\", \"applies\": \"limit 10\", \"rationale\": \"...\"}
  ]
}

ACCEPTANCE
- 'cofferdam advise src/foo.ts' emits a JSON object listing layer membership, applicable rule IDs, and rationale snippets.
- 'cofferdam advise --format text src/foo.ts' is human-readable.
- 'cofferdam advise src/' recurses and emits one record per file (line-delim JSON for machine consumption).
- Glob support: 'cofferdam advise \"src/**/*.ts\"' works.
- Non-zero exit only on internal error; absence of constraints is not an error (a file with no applicable rules emits a record with constraints: []).
- Spot check on bestefforttools: a file in a configured layer returns the layer it's in and a non-empty rule list including layer / orphan-export / complexity rules as applicable.
- Performance budget: under 200ms for a single file on the bestefforttools tree (uses warm graph from a single engine pass).

IMPLEMENTATION NOTES
- Reuses the existing check registry: filter to rules whose meta() applies to the file's extension.
- Uses the freshly-merged graph (cofferdam-engine/src/graph.rs) for layer lookup, OrphanExport applicability, etc.
- Reads cofferdam.invariants.toml when that bead lands; until then reads existing cofferdam.toml [layers].
- Plugin checks can opt in via a new optional method on the Check trait — rough shape: 'fn advise(&self, file_meta: &FileMeta) -> Option<AdvisorySpec>'. If unimplemented, a check's advisory surface is just its meta() rationale + its parameters from config.

OUT OF SCOPE
- --diff (separate child bead).
- MCP wrapping (separate child bead at P4).
- Plugin advisory hooks beyond the default fallback to meta() + config — file as a follow-up if plugin authors ask for richer advisory output.
- Persistent advisory cache. If single-file advise takes more than ~200ms on bestefforttools-scale repos, file a separate bead.

title: [epic] cofferdam-as-context-substrate
description:
Move cofferdam from a linter that runs after the fact to an architectural-specification, enforcement, and agent-context substrate for a TypeScript codebase. The primitives are already in place — project graph (cd-7h5), plugin SDK (cd-81a, in flight), robot mode (cd-yvm), severity gating, baselines, --since. This epic wires the agent-facing surfaces that turn those primitives into a first-class tool in agentic edit loops.

STRATEGIC FRAMING
Today cofferdam is positioned as 'a TypeScript code-quality analyzer'; the comparison set is ESLint and Biome. After this epic, the comparison set is ADR systems plus architecture-as-code tools — neither of which actually enforces anything. The differentiator is that cofferdam has executable opinions, a project graph, AND an agent-queryable advisory surface in one tool. No other tool in the TS lint space treats the LLM agent as a first-class consumer of architectural constraints.

The plugin SDK reframes accordingly: it is not 'write custom lint rules,' it is 'codify your team's architectural decisions as executable, agent-queryable specifications.'

WHY THIS, WHY NOW
Agentic edit loops expose the gap. An LLM agent walking into a codebase has cold-start context — it cannot read CLAUDE.md every session. Today an agent learns architectural rules by violating them; cofferdam's findings only fire AFTER bad code exists. The valuable mode for agents is BEFORE the fact: 'here are the constraints on the file you're about to touch.' That is what 'advise' does, and it is the load-bearing primitive for everything else in this epic.

CHILDREN
1. cofferdam advise <path> — JIT architectural advisory (P2, must-have)
2. cofferdam advise --diff <ref> — pre-flight validation for proposed changes (P3, depends on #1)
3. cofferdam.invariants.toml — promote layer config to project-wide architectural spec (P2)
4. cofferdam-mcp server — native MCP integration (P4, deprioritized)

OUT OF SCOPE FOR THIS EPIC
- Type-aware advisory (full ts-morph integration). Phase 5 territory.
- Cross-language support. Tracked separately as the platform/TS split (see design/platform-extensibility.md).
- Persistent advisory cache for huge projects. If 'advise' is too slow on bestefforttools-scale repos, file as a follow-up bead.
- IDE integration via cofferdam-lsp. The LSP can consume the same advisory data once the CLI shape is stable.

DEPENDS ON
- cd-7h5 (project graph) — already CLOSED. The graph is what 'advise' reads to compute layer membership and applicable rules.
- cd-81a (plugin SDK) — helpful but not strictly blocking. Built-in rules can advise on day one; plugin participation in advisory output is a follow-up enhancement.

ACCEPTANCE FOR THE EPIC
- cofferdam ships an 'advise' subcommand that an agent can shell out to before editing a file.
- cofferdam.invariants.toml is the canonical artifact for architectural intent — readable by humans and machines, consumed by multiple checks.
- The MCP server (when it lands at P4) makes cofferdam queryable from any MCP-enabled agent runtime without the agent carrying cofferdam knowledge in its context.

- Emit SARIF 2.1.0: $schema, version, runs[].tool.driver { name, version, informationUri, rules[] }, runs[].results[] with ruleId, level (note/warning/error mapped from Severity), message.text, locations[].physicalLocation { artifactLocation.uri, region { startLine, startColumn, endLine, endColumn } }, and partialFingerprints for stable result identity across runs.

- Register in cofferdam-formatters/src/lib.rs and add 'sarif' variant to OutputFormat enum + Cmd::Check match in cofferdam-cli/src/main.rs.
- Update docs/output-formats.md and docs/ci-recipes.md with a SARIF + github/codeql-action/upload-sarif example.
- Fixture-based test: snapshot a SARIF run for examples/triple_equals.ts.

Acceptance:

- GitHub Action workflow can upload it via codeql-action/upload-sarif and findings appear on the PR (manual smoke test, documented in ci-recipes).

title: Design.LayerViolation — declarative layering rules in cofferdam.toml
description:
Let users declare a layer hierarchy in cofferdam.toml and flag imports that cross it.

EXAMPLE CONFIG:
[layers]
infra  = ["src/infra/**"]
domain = ["src/domain/**"]
app    = ["src/app/**"]

[layers.allow]
domain = ["infra"]                  # domain may import from infra
app    = ["domain", "infra"]        # app may import from both

A 'domain' file importing from 'app' fires a finding. Inverse direction (app → domain) is allowed because 'domain' appears in app's allow list.

Reads imports table built by the graph epic; checks each edge against the declared rules.

Edge cases:
- Files outside any declared layer: configurable (default: ignore).
- Symbolic re-exports through barrel files: walk to the deepest definition's layer.
- Test layer: convention is to allow tests to import from anything; provide a 'test' layer with implicit allow=*.
notes: Child of cd-7h5. The most opinionated of the graph checks; needs the cofferdam.toml options system mature (cd-4ms — already closed).

title: Design.ImportCycle — circular import chains
description:
Flag any cycle in the import graph: A imports B, B imports C, C imports A. Tarjan's SCC over the import graph; emit one finding per cycle with all participating files in 'related' spans.

Configurable max-depth (default unlimited — find all cycles regardless of length). Configurable severity threshold by length (length-2 cycles are usually bugs; length-N≥5 cycles are arch debt).

Type-only imports excluded from cycle detection by default (TS allows type-only cycles cleanly via 'import type'). Configurable.

Output ordering: deterministic — start each cycle from its alphabetically-lowest filename so re-runs produce identical reports.
notes: Child of cd-7h5. Sonnet-friendly once graph lands.

title: Design.OrphanExport — exported but never imported anywhere in project
description:
Flag any export (named, default, type) that no other file imports. Common dead-code source after refactors. Project-wide so single-file checks (tsconfig noUnusedLocals) miss it.

Reads the imports/exports tables built in pass 1 by the graph epic. Emit one finding per orphan export at the export site; no related spans needed.

Edge cases:
- Test files: configurable inclusion (default: skip *_test.ts, *.test.ts, *.spec.ts so test-only exports aren't flagged as orphans).
- Public API entry points: configurable allowlist (default: package.json 'main'/'module'/'exports' targets are NEVER flagged).
- Re-exports through barrel files: the export at the deepest definition is the orphan, not the re-export. Walk the chain.
- Type-only exports: same rule applies; type-only imports count as imports.

title: [epic] Project knowledge graph + graph-aware checks
description:
Build a typed project graph (imports, exports, references, type relations) in pass 1, expose it via CorpusIndex for graph-aware checks in pass 2. The graph is the strategic differentiator versus Credo and ESLint — none of the existing TS linters offer this depth of cross-file reasoning.

DEPENDS ON: cd-d1y (two-pass infrastructure must land first).

GRAPH CONSTRUCTION (pass 1):
- Module resolver (oxc_resolver already a dep) builds an import graph keyed by absolute path.
- Per-file exports table: named exports, default export, re-exports, type-only exports.
- Per-file imports table: source module, imported names, type-only flag.
- Reference index: for each exported symbol, the set of files that import it.

CHILD BEADS (each one sonnet-friendly once the graph exists):
1. Design.OrphanExport — declared, never imported anywhere in the project.
2. Design.ImportCycle — circular import chains (depth N configurable).
3. Design.LayerViolation — declarative layer config in cofferdam.toml; flag imports that cross declared boundaries.
4. Refactor.DeadExport — exported but every consumer marks the import as type-only or never references the symbol after import.
5. Warning.UnusedImport — already common in TS but worth emitting at the project level so single-file checks (like a tsconfig noUnusedLocals) don't miss re-export passthroughs.

OUT OF SCOPE FOR THIS EPIC:
- Type-aware graph (full ts-morph integration) — that's the existing phase 5 work.
- Call graph (function-call resolution) — separate, much harder.
- Cross-file rename safety — IDE/LSP work.

This is the leapfrog over Credo. Credo's two-pass is mostly used for stylistic consistency; the same infrastructure can power genuine architectural analysis when paired with a proper graph.

title: Auto-generated check catalog → VitePress site
description:
Switch the check catalog from a hand-maintained `docs/checks.md` (landed in cd-m3g) to a fully generated artifact set, with a VitePress site as the human-facing renderer. Keep code as the only source of truth — `CheckMeta` plus a per-check companion markdown body — and emit machine-readable artifacts that AI agents will be the primary consumer of.

## Source of truth

- `CheckMeta` in Rust (existing) → metadata: id, category, priority, severity, options, requires_types, consistency, explanation.
- New: per-check companion markdown at `crates/cofferdam-checks/docs/<id>.md`. Loaded into `CheckMeta` via `body: &'static str = include_str!("../docs/<id>.md")`.
  - Body is the long-form prose: motivation, bad/good examples, deliberate non-flagged shapes, related checks.
  - Build-script (or doc-test) assertion: every entry in `all_builtins()` has a companion file present; failing companion = compile error.
  - Seed content from `docs/checks.md` (cd-m3g) — split into per-check files in the same commit that wires the include_str!.

## Generated artifacts

One subcommand, multiple outputs, all from the same iteration over `all_builtins()`:

```
cofferdam gen-docs --out=docs/
```

Emits:

1. **`docs/checks.json`** — schema-stable index. Array of `{ id, category, priority, severity, options, requires_types, consistency, explanation, body, examples_url }`. Hosted at a stable URL (e.g. `https://cofferdam.dev/checks.json`). The canonical machine artifact for agents.
2. **`docs/checks/<id>.md`** — one file per check, with frontmatter (`id`, `category`, `priority`, `severity`, `options`) plus the body text. Consumed by VitePress.
3. **`docs/checks/index.md`** — generated landing page grouped by category, links to each check.
4. **`docs/llms.txt`** — root index in the [llms.txt](https://llmstxt.org) format. Curated entry points: install snippet, catalog index URL, JSON URL, key CLI flags.

CI gate: `cofferdam gen-docs --check` re-runs the generator against the committed `docs/` and fails if anything would change. Same shape as `cargo fmt --check`.

## Website (VitePress)

- New directory: `website/` (or `docs-site/` — bikeshed at implementation).
- VitePress consumes `docs/checks/*.md` directly. Sidebar auto-generated from category frontmatter. Local search enabled (no Algolia).
- Default theme; minimal customisation. The site is a renderer, not a brand surface.
- Deploy via GitHub Actions to GitHub Pages (cofferdam.github.io/cofferdam) or to Vercel under a chosen domain. Decide at implementation time — both are CI-friendly.
- Versioning: out of scope for v1. Path-based versioning (`/v0.1/checks/...`) once we hit 1.0.

## Why VitePress

Picked over Astro Starlight, Docusaurus, mdBook because the catalog is a pure docs site (no marketing landing page, no interactive components today), VitePress is purpose-built for that use case with the lowest config-to-result ratio, and Vite-fast incremental builds matter when `cofferdam gen-docs` re-runs on every check change.

If we ever need interactive components (e.g. wasm "try cofferdam in your browser"), revisit and migrate to Astro Starlight — both produce static HTML, so the agent-readability story is unchanged.

## Acceptance

- `crates/cofferdam-checks/docs/<id>.md` exists for every entry in `all_builtins()`. Build fails (or `cargo test` fails) if a companion is missing.
- `cofferdam gen-docs --out=docs/` produces `checks.json`, `checks/<id>.md` per check, `checks/index.md`, `llms.txt`. Idempotent: running twice in a row produces no diff.
- CI workflow runs `cofferdam gen-docs --check` and fails on drift.
- VitePress site builds successfully, serves the catalog at a stable URL, has working local search and a sitemap.
- `docs/checks.md` (the hand-written cd-m3g page) is replaced by the generated `docs/checks/index.md` — same anchors and content, no broken inbound links.
- `cofferdam explain <id>` keeps working (already sources from `CheckMeta`); the long-form `body` becomes available via a future `--full` flag (separate bead).

## Out of scope (separate beads)

- `cofferdam explain --full` flag rendering the markdown body (cd-brp follow-up).
- Versioning of the published site.
- Marketing landing page on the same domain.
- Custom theme work beyond the VitePress default.

title: Engine: two-pass mode for consistency checks
description:
Add a generalized two-pass mode to the engine: pass 1 collects evidence, pass 2 emits findings against the collected baseline. Canary check: Consistency.QuoteStyle.

The infrastructure reuses the existing CorpusIndex slot pattern (already used by Design.DuplicateExportName, Refactor.DuplicateBlock) but adds an explicit pass-2 hook on the Check trait — finalize-style — so consistency checks can declare 'I need to see all files before emitting'.

Scope:
- Engine pass-2 hook on Check trait (sibling to finalize, but per-file rather than corpus-wide).
- Pass-1 evidence storage via existing CorpusIndex.
- Consistency.QuoteStyle as the canary: count single vs double quotes per file, emit findings against the dominant style.
- Threshold for 'dominant' = strict majority (>50%); per-file scope (not project-wide). Both decisions can be revisited via OptionSpec later.

EXPLICITLY OUT OF SCOPE — handled by separate epic 'Project knowledge graph':
- Project-wide imports/exports/references graph.
- Graph-aware checks (orphan exports, cycles, layering, dead code).
- Cross-file rename safety.

Two-pass infra is a prereq for the graph epic but the graph design is not bundled here. Keep the pass-2 hook generic enough that a future graph builder (running in pass 1) can expose its results via the same CorpusIndex pattern.

title: Warning pack: NoConsoleLog + NoDebugger + NoEval
description: Three AST-only single-node visitor checks following the existing Warning.TripleEquals recipe in crates/cofferdam-checks/src/warning.rs. (1) NoConsoleLog: match CallExpression where callee is MemberExpression{object:Identifier('console'),property:Identifier(_)}. Default Low severity, base_priority -10. (2) NoDebugger: match DebuggerStatement (even simpler). (3) NoEval: match CallExpression where callee is Identifier('eval') OR MemberExpression{object:Identifier('Function'),property:Identifier('prototype')}. Default High severity (universal security ban). One fixture per check in examples/. Register all three in crates/cofferdam-checks/src/lib.rs::all_builtins(). Parallel-safe: each check is its own struct — can fan out via subagents per CLAUDE.md dispatch rules. Three checks, one bead.
close_reason: Implemented Warning.NoConsoleLog (any console.X call, base_priority -10, severity Low), Warning.NoDebugger (DebuggerStatement, priority 10, Medium), and Warning.NoEval (eval() and new Function(), priority 18, High). Three fixtures in examples/. Real-repo validation: bestefforttools surfaces 75 genuine console calls + 0 debugger + 0 eval, zero false positives spot-checked. 214 tests pass, clippy/fmt clean.

title: [v1] .cofferdamignore — promote from 'wired but invisible' to a documented v1 feature
description:
The wiring already exists ('discover.rs:76' uses the ignore crate's 'add_custom_ignore_filename(".cofferdamignore")', so full gitignore-syntax including negation works today). What's missing for v1 is everything around it: discovery, scaffolding, documentation, config interaction, and the policy on what to ignore vs baseline vs cache.

Acceptance:

1. Documentation
   - Dedicated page 'docs/configuration/ignoring-files.md' (under VitePress site, cd-t6n) covering: gitignore-syntax (incl. negation with !), precedence vs .gitignore, vs CLI '--no-ignore', vs per-check 'exclude' globs in cofferdam.toml. Worked examples: ignore vendored dirs, ignore generated *.gen.ts, un-ignore a single file inside an ignored dir.
   - npm README (cd-dh4) gains a 4-line snippet showing creating a '.cofferdamignore' to scope past 'dist/'.
   - 'cofferdam check --help' line for '--no-ignore' updated to mention both filenames + link.

2. First-run scaffolding ('cofferdam init', cd-fnm)
   - 'init' writes a starter '.cofferdamignore' with commented-out common entries: 'node_modules/', 'dist/', 'build/', 'coverage/', '*.generated.ts', '*.gen.ts', '__generated__/', 'storybook-static/'. Commented so users opt-in line-by-line and see what would be plausibly ignored — not a wall of muted lines.
   - If '.cofferdamignore' already exists: 'init' leaves it alone (never overwrites).

3. Diagnostics ('cofferdam doctor', cd-oa3)
   - Doctor reports: '.cofferdamignore present at <path>', and the count of files it excludes from the default scope ('N files in src/ ignored by .cofferdamignore'). High-value signal — users frequently misconfigure this and don't notice until findings disappear.

4. Config interaction ('cofferdam.toml', cd-4ms)
   - cd-4ms acceptance grows an '[ignore]' section: '[ignore] paths = ["foo/**", "!foo/keep.ts"]'. Globs append to '.cofferdamignore' patterns at engine level (not file-merged on disk). Documented precedence: CLI '--no-ignore' > '[ignore].paths' in TOML > '.cofferdamignore' > '.gitignore' > defaults.
   - File this scope-bump as a comment/note on cd-4ms; do NOT file a separate bead (one config file, one loader bead).

5. Baseline / cache placement policy (resolves the gap in cd-fnm and cd-d31)
   - Canonical layout: '.cofferdam/baseline.json' (committed) and '.cofferdam/cache/' (gitignored). 'cofferdam init' writes '.gitignore' entries for '.cofferdam/cache/' specifically, NOT the whole '.cofferdam/' directory.
   - '.cofferdamignore' itself is a regular project file: committed, NOT in any ignore list.
   - Documented in 'docs/configuration/baselines.md' and 'docs/configuration/ignoring-files.md'.

6. Verification
   - Smoke test: bestefforttools with no '.cofferdamignore' → N findings; add '.cofferdamignore' with 'app/components/legacy/**' → N - K findings, K matching the legacy-dir count. Asserts engine respects the file end-to-end (already does, but lock the contract with a test).
   - Test: negation pattern works (ignore 'vendor/**' but un-ignore 'vendor/keep.ts').
   - Test: '--no-ignore' flag bypasses both '.gitignore' AND '.cofferdamignore' (matches the help text).

Cross-links:
- cd-4ms (extend with [ignore] section)
- cd-fnm (init seeds starter file + .gitignore policy)
- cd-oa3 (doctor surfaces ignore state)
- cd-t6n / cd-b3k (docs site page)
- cd-dh4 (npm README mention)

Design note: per-check ignore globs ('[checks.Readability.MaxLineLength] exclude = [...]') are out of scope here — that's cd-81a.5 (declarative file scoping). '.cofferdamignore' is the broad-stroke 'pretend these files don't exist' lever; per-check scoping is the surgical lever. Both ship; they don't compete.

title: [CI] cofferdam-check GitHub composite Action
description:
The diagram's CI/BUILD STEP quadrant currently demands users hand-roll a workflow with pnpm setup + cofferdam invocation. A composite Action collapses that to one 'uses:' block — the standard pattern for any CLI that wants to live in CI. This is the single biggest UX win for the build-step story without waiting for SARIF/phase-6.

Acceptance:
- New repo (or path under this repo): 'TAJD/cofferdam-action' as a public composite GitHub Action. If a separate repo, mirror tags from cofferdam (v0.1.4 → cofferdam-action@v0.1.4 + a moving v1 tag).
- 'action.yml' inputs: paths (default 'src/'), since (default ''), fail-on (default 'medium'), baseline (default '.cofferdam/baseline.json'), version (default 'latest'), config (default 'cofferdam.toml').
- Steps: download the matching cofferdam binary from GitHub Releases (no npm install — composite Action should be standalone, not require Node). Use the platform of the runner. Cache by version key.
- Run cofferdam check with the resolved flags. Capture JSON output.
- Translate findings to GitHub workflow commands ('::error file=...,line=...,col=...,title=<check_id>::<message>') so devs see red squiggles on the PR diff WITHOUT SARIF wiring. This is the v1 substitute for cd-x6? (SARIF, phase 6).
- Exit with the binary's exit code so the job goes red on findings ≥ fail-on.
- README example: 5-line workflow that any TS repo can paste.
- Smoke test in this repo: a workflow that uses the action against examples/ and asserts annotations are emitted.

Depends on cd-d31 (--baseline), cd-3pn (--since), cd-t1a (--fail-on) — all flags the action wraps.

Design note: composite Action over JS Action because we don't want to ship a Node runtime when the cofferdam binary is the actual workload. Composite means each step is shell + the binary; smaller surface, easier to audit.
close_reason: Composite GitHub Action shipped. .github/actions/cofferdam-check/action.yml + README.md + smoke workflow .github/workflows/action-smoke.yml. Inputs: paths/fail-on/baseline/since/version/config (CLI flag names verified against crates/cofferdam-cli/src/main.rs). Asset naming derives from release.yml's tagged-archive scheme (cofferdam-v${tag}-${target}). Findings parsed from --robot --format=json and emitted as native ::error/::warning workflow annotations — no SARIF wiring needed for v1. Marketplace publishing intentionally out of scope (no branding:).

title: [Docs site] Generated CLI reference + check catalog (drift-proof via CI)
description:
Generate two doc surfaces from the source of truth so they cannot drift: the CLI reference (from clap) and the per-check catalog (from CheckMeta). If hand-written, both go stale within weeks.

Acceptance:
- New subcommand 'cofferdam docs export --out <dir>'. Walks all_builtins() and writes one Markdown file per category to <dir>/checks/{consistency,design,readability,refactor,warning}.md. Each entry: id, default severity, default priority, explanation (from CheckMeta), default options (if any), one good/bad example pulled from examples/<fixture>.ts (so the example is the same file the test suite exercises).
- Same subcommand also writes <dir>/reference/cli.md by recursing the clap Command tree (use the 'clap-markdown' crate, ~5-line integration; or hand-roll if it doesn't render the way we want).
- Closes the implementation side of cd-m3g (check catalog) and cd-l32 (output formats — that one becomes a hand-written reference page that the generator does NOT touch, since it's prose, not enum-derived).
- New CI step in ci.yml after build/test: run 'cofferdam docs export --out docs/' and fail if 'git diff --exit-code docs/checks docs/reference/cli.md' is non-empty. This is the structural guarantee against drift.
- Local workflow: contributors run the export themselves before pushing if they edited a check or a flag. Document this in CONTRIBUTING.md (and create CONTRIBUTING.md if missing — keep it small).

Depends on cd-g4y umbrella; coordinates with cd-m3g (which becomes 'curate the prose intro at the top of each generated category file' rather than 'write all 5 files by hand').

Design note: generated content lives between explicit '<!-- BEGIN GENERATED -->' / '<!-- END GENERATED -->' markers in each file so the human-written intro at the top of each category page survives regeneration. The export command rewrites only between those markers.
close_reason: Absorbed into cd-cgw Phase 2+3. The clap-markdown-driven CLI reference at docs/reference/cli.md ships as one of cofferdam gen-docs' 5 artifact types — same generator, single CI gate (cofferdam gen-docs --check). The cross-category checks markdown was already covered by cd-cgw's per-check files at docs/checks/<id>.md (one per check, frontmatter-driven, AUTOGENERATED comment). cd-b3k's <!-- BEGIN GENERATED --> marker concept was not needed because each generated file is fully autogenerated (no hand-written intro to preserve).

title: Rewrite packages/cofferdam/README.md for the install-and-include-in-build user story
description:
Today's npm package README is 55 lines and stops at 'pnpm exec cofferdam check src/'. After the adoption-unlock features land, the npm README is the single most-read doc — it's what shows on npmjs.com. Must walk a new user from install → first useful CI step in under 60 seconds of reading.

Acceptance:
- Sections in this order:
  1. 30-second pitch (what + why, 3 lines)
  2. Install (pnpm/npm/yarn one-liner each)
  3. First run: 'cofferdam init' walkthrough — what it creates, what to commit
  4. The five built-in checks at a glance (table — link to full catalog)
  5. CI integration: GitHub Actions snippet using --since + --fail-on; husky pre-commit snippet
  6. Configuration: minimal cofferdam.toml example covering disable-a-check, change-a-limit, scope-a-glob
  7. Suppression: one example each of next-line and block disable
  8. Exit codes table
  9. Sandboxed installs / --ignore-scripts (existing content, kept)

title: Add Refactor.DuplicateBlock (DRY) check
description: New check: detect near-identical statement blocks across files in a single cofferdam run. Likely approach: token/AST hashing of statement runs above a minimum size (>= N tokens OR >= M statements), bucket-and-compare to find duplicates, emit one Issue per duplicate set referencing all locations. Open design questions (resolve in a child design doc before implementation): (1) hash granularity — raw tokens vs. canonicalised AST (rename-resilient)? (2) cross-file engine API — does CheckContext expose a corpus, or do we need an aggregator pass? (3) thresholds + how to surface the N>2 case in the Issue model. Plan first, then implement.
design:
## Decisions

- Detection modes: AST canonicalised hashing (default ON) + token-stream hashing (opt-in flag include_tokens).
- Engine integration: aggregator pattern via the typed shared-corpus API delivered by cd-0ps.
- Issue model: one issue per duplicate set. Uses Issue.related: Vec<Span> (delivered by cd-0ps).
- Defaults: min_statements = 6, min_tokens = 50 (used by token mode), include_tokens = false, include_ast = true. All four configurable via cofferdam.toml once cd-4ms lands; for now, hardcoded with constructor args.
- Canonicalisation: identifier names replaced with per-block locals ($0, $1 ...); literals KEPT literal-sensitive at v1 (=== 5 not equal === 6) to avoid noise. Revisit after bestefforttools validation.

## Cross-file API (delivered by cd-0ps)

cd-0ps lands a typed-key shared corpus. DuplicateBlock uses it like:

    pub static DUPLICATE_FINGERPRINTS: CorpusKey<Vec<Fingerprint>> =
        CorpusKey::new("Refactor.DuplicateBlock.fingerprints");

    impl Check for DuplicateBlock {
        fn run(&self, file, ctx) -> Vec<Issue> {
            ctx.corpus.with_slot(&DUPLICATE_FINGERPRINTS, |fps| {
                fps.extend(self.fingerprints_for(file));
            });
            Vec::new()
        }
        fn finalize(&self, ctx) -> Vec<Issue> {
            let mut out = Vec::new();
            ctx.corpus.with_slot(&DUPLICATE_FINGERPRINTS, |fps| {
                out = aggregate_duplicates(fps);
            });
            out
        }
    }

A Fingerprint is { hash: u64, kind: AstHash | TokenHash, file_id: u32, span: Span }. Two checks could share a slot by reusing the same CorpusKey; DuplicateBlock owns its own slot.

## Implementation steps

### Step 1 — cd-0ps engine prerequisite (separate issue)

Delivers: corpus module, CorpusKey<T>, CorpusIndex, CheckContext.corpus, FinalizeContext, breaking finalize signature, Issue.related, formatter wiring. Single-agent, blocks this issue.

### Step 2 — DuplicateBlock skeleton

Replace any stub in crates/cofferdam-checks/src/refactor.rs. Struct holds the four config fields. META: id Refactor.DuplicateBlock, category Refactor, base_priority 12, options listing min_statements / min_tokens / include_tokens / include_ast.

Define DUPLICATE_FINGERPRINTS as a module-level CorpusKey constant.

### Step 3 — AST mode (default on)

In Check::run when include_ast:

- Visit Program, walk every BlockStatement and Program body.
- Slide a window of min_statements consecutive Statement nodes.
- Canonicalise: walk the subtree; map each IdentifierReference / BindingIdentifier / IdentifierName to a stable index based on first occurrence within the window. Keep literal values verbatim. Drop spans/comments from the hash input.
- Hash with twox-hash::Xxh3 (or std DefaultHasher to start; perf-tune later).
- Push Fingerprint { hash, kind: AstHash, file_id, span } into the corpus slot via ctx.corpus.with_slot.

Check::run returns empty.

### Step 4 — Token mode (opt-in)

Only runs when include_tokens. Slide an N-token window over the file lexer output, canonicalise identifiers to id and literals to lit, hash, push as kind: TokenHash.

### Step 5 — finalize() implementation

- ctx.corpus.with_slot(&DUPLICATE_FINGERPRINTS, |fps| ...).
- Group by hash.
- For each group with len >= 2: sort spans by (file_path, start_byte); pick first as primary; rest become Issue.related; emit one Issue per group.
- Dedupe overlapping spans across modes (an AST-mode hit and a token-mode hit covering the same byte range collapse into the AST one).

### Step 6 — Fixtures

- examples/duplicate_block.ts: two functions with structurally-identical bodies but different param + local names should flag. One distinct function should NOT flag. One short helper under min_statements should NOT flag.
- examples/duplicate_block_tokens.ts: repeated multi-line expression that AST mode misses because it spans non-statement boundaries should flag ONLY with include_tokens.

### Step 7 — Verification

Per CLAUDE.md verification block: cargo build/test/clippy/fmt + cargo run on the fixture. After implementation, run on C:/Users/tajdi/bestefforttools and capture the top 10 findings before handing off to cd-3ax.

title: Robot mode — compact line-delim format
description:
JSON output (cd-yvm) is functional but 1.85x text mode bytes due to repeated field names per finding (366 findings × full schema = bloat). For real token economy, ship a one-finding-per-line pipe-delimited format alongside JSON.

Proposed: `--format=compact` emits a single header line + one record per finding:

```
priority|severity|category|id|file|line|column|message
-5|warning|readability|Readability.MaxLineLength|examples/sample.ts|8|121|line is 149 characters, exceeds limit of 120
```

- Stable header — parsers split on pipe
- Messages with literal pipes get backslash-escaped
- Well-formed even when zero findings (header only)

- 200-finding run produces output ≤ 35% of text formatter's bytes (and ≤ 50% of JSON)
- Header documented at `docs/output-formats.md`

close_reason: Implemented --format=compact: pipe-delimited line-per-finding format with stable 8-column header (priority|severity|category|id|file|line|column|message).
